title: 2 Samuel

stories.title: ⚔️ 2 Samuel 1
summaryBullets: After the death of Saul, David returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites and stayed in Ziklag two days. (1:1).
On the third day a man with torn clothes and dust on his head arrived from Saul’s camp. When he came to David, he fell to the ground to pay him homage. (1:2).
“Where have you come from?” David asked. “I have escaped from the Israelite camp,” he replied. (1:3).
“What was the outcome?” David asked. “Please tell me.” “The troops fled from the battle,” he replied. “Many of them fell and died. And Saul and his son Jonathan are also dead.” (1:4).
Then David asked the young man who had brought him the report, “How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?” (1:5).
“I happened to be on Mount Gilboa,” he replied, “and there was Saul, leaning on his spear, with the chariots and the cavalry closing in on him. (1:6).
When he turned around and saw me, he called out to me, and I answered, ‘Here I am!’ (1:7).
‘Who are you?’ he asked. So I told him, ‘I am an Amalekite.’ (1:8).
Then he begged me, ‘Stand over me and kill me, for agony has seized me, but my life still lingers.’ (1:9).

So I stood over him and killed him, because I knew that after he had fallen he could not survive. And I took the crown that was on his head and the band that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord.” (1:10).
Then David took hold of his own clothes and tore them, and all the men who were with him did the same. (1:11).
They mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and his son Jonathan, and for the people of the LORD and the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword. (1:12).
And David inquired of the young man who had brought him the report, “Where are you from?” “I am the son of a foreigner,” he answered. “I am an Amalekite.” (1:13).
So David asked him, “Why were you not afraid to lift your hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?” (1:14).
Then David summoned one of the young men and said, “Go, execute him!” So the young man struck him down, and he died. (1:15).
For David had said to the Amalekite, “Your blood be on your own head because your own mouth has testified against you, saying, ‘I killed the LORD’s anointed.’” (1:16).
Then David took up this lament for Saul and his son Jonathan, (1:17).
and he ordered that the sons of Judah be taught the Song of the Bow. It is written in the Book of Jashar: (1:18).
“Your glory, O Israel, lies slain on your heights. How the mighty have fallen! (1:19).
Tell it not in Gath; proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, and the daughters of the uncircumcised exult. (1:20).
O mountains of Gilboa, may you have no dew or rain, no fields yielding offerings of grain. For there the shield of the mighty was defiled, the shield of Saul, no longer anointed with oil. (1:21).
From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan did not retreat, and the sword of Saul did not return empty. (1:22).
Saul and Jonathan, beloved and delightful in life, were not divided in death. They were swifter than eagles; they were stronger than lions. (1:23).
O daughters of Israel, weep for Saul, who clothed you in scarlet and luxury, who decked your garments with ornaments of gold. (1:24).
How the mighty have fallen in the thick of battle! Jonathan lies slain on your heights. (1:25).
I grieve for you, Jonathan, my brother. You were delightful to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women. (1:26).
How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!” (1:27).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 31:1-6: Saul's actual death on Gilboa, where he falls on his own sword and his armour-bearer follows him.
1 Samuel 24:6: David refuses to stretch out his hand against the LORD's anointed, even with Saul in reach.
Joshua 10:12-13: The sun stands still over Gibeon, and the account is said to be written in the Book of Jashar.
Micah 1:10: Tell it not in Gath, weep not at all, the same words taken up by the prophet generations later.
1 Samuel 18:1-4: Jonathan's soul is knit to David's, and he gives him his robe, his sword, his bow, and his belt.

translationNotes.note: The Amalekite in verse 10 does not bring news, he brings the regalia, and that is the whole of his play. A nezer is the band worn round the head that marked a man as consecrated to an office; the high priest wears one of gold (Exodus 29:6), and Joash is crowned with one at 2 Kings 11:12. Handing the nezer and the arm-band to David is handing him the kingship, and the man plainly expects to be paid for it.

Mashiach means smeared with oil, and it is a job title rather than a compliment: the man God has installed by having oil poured over his head. David uses it in verses 14 and 16 as the ground for executing the man who claims to have finished Saul off, and the lament turns the same image inside out at verse 21, calling Saul's shield defiled, no longer anointed with oil, which is the ordinary treatment for keeping a leather shield supple.

A qinah is a formal funeral song with its own limping rhythm, chanted at a burial and often led by women hired for the purpose (Jeremiah 9:17-20). It is a public composition, not private grief: David's is titled the Song of the Bow, ordered to be taught to the men of Judah, and written down. The whole book of Lamentations is five of them, and the prophets use the form to sing over a nation before it falls (Ezekiel 19:1, Amos 5:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּנוֹת פְּלִשְׁתִּים (benot Pelishtim), the daughters of the Philistines
translationNotes.note: Verse 20 is not about secrecy but about a specific scene David can picture. Women came out to meet a returning army with drums and a sung refrain, which is exactly how he himself had been greeted at 1 Samuel 18:6-7. He is imagining the same custom performed in Gath and Ashkelon over Saul's body. Gath and Ashkelon are two of the five Philistine cities, both within a day or two of the Judean border.
Lost non-canonical collection of heroic songs (also cited in Joshua 10:13).

stories.keyTakeaway: An Amalekite messenger brings David news that Saul and Jonathan are dead and claims he killed Saul at his request; David executes the messenger and composes an elaborate lament mourning Saul and Jonathan.

headings.text: David’s Song for Saul and Jonathan

stories.title: ⚔️ 2 Samuel 2
summaryBullets: Some time later, David inquired of the LORD, “Should I go up to one of the towns of Judah?” “Go up,” the LORD answered. Then David asked, “Where should I go?” “To Hebron,” replied the LORD. (2:1).
So David went there with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel. (2:2).
David also took the men who were with him, each with his household, and they settled in the towns near Hebron. (2:3).
Then the men of Judah came to Hebron, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. And they told David, “It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul.” (2:4).
So David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead to tell them, “The LORD bless you, because you showed this kindness to Saul your lord when you buried him. (2:5).
Now may the LORD show you loving devotion and faithfulness, and I will also show you the same favor because you have done this. (2:6).
Now then, be strong and courageous, for though Saul your lord is dead, the house of Judah has anointed me as their king.” (2:7).
Meanwhile, Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul’s army, took Saul’s son Ish-bosheth, moved him to Mahanaim, (2:8).
and made him king over Gilead, Asher, Jezreel, Ephraim, and Benjamin— over all Israel. (2:9).
Saul’s son Ish-bosheth was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for two years. The house of Judah, however, followed David. (2:10).
And the length of time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months. (2:11).
One day Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul marched out from Mahanaim to Gibeon. (2:12).
So Joab son of Zeruiah and the servants of David marched out and met them by the pool of Gibeon. And the two groups took up positions on opposite sides of the pool. (2:13).
Then Abner said to Joab, “Let us have the young men get up and compete before us.” “Let them get up,” Joab replied. (2:14).
So they got up and were counted off — twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve for David. (2:15).
Then each man grabbed his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his opponent’s side, and they all fell together. So this place, which is in Gibeon, is called Helkath-hazzurim. (2:16).
The battle that day was intense, and Abner and the men of Israel were defeated by the servants of David. (2:17).
The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was fleet of foot like a wild gazelle, (2:18).
and he chased Abner, not turning to the right or to the left in his pursuit. (2:19).
And Abner glanced back and said, “Is that you, Asahel?” “It is,” Asahel replied. (2:20).
So Abner told him, “Turn to your right or to your left, seize one of the young men, and take his equipment for yourself.” But Asahel would not stop chasing him. (2:21).
Once again, Abner warned Asahel, “Stop chasing me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How could I show my face to your brother Joab?” (2:22).

But Asahel refused to turn away. So Abner thrust the butt of his spear into his stomach, and it came out his back, and he fell dead on the spot. And every man paused when he came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died. (2:23).
But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. By sunset, they had gone as far as the hill of Ammah opposite Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon. (2:24).
The Benjamites rallied to Abner, formed a single unit, and took their stand atop a hill. (2:25).
Then Abner called out to Joab: “Must the sword devour forever? Do you not realize that this will only end in bitterness? How long before you tell the troops to stop pursuing their brothers?” (2:26).
“As surely as God lives,” Joab replied, “if you had not spoken up, the troops would have continued pursuing their brothers until morning.” (2:27).
So Joab blew the ram’s horn, and all the troops stopped; they no longer pursued Israel or continued to fight. (2:28).
And all that night Abner and his men marched through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan, marched all morning, and arrived at Mahanaim. (2:29).
When Joab returned from pursuing Abner, he gathered all the troops. In addition to Asahel, nineteen of David’s servants were missing, (2:30).
but they had struck down 360 Benjamites who were with Abner. (2:31).
And they took Asahel and buried him in his father’s tomb in Bethlehem. Then Joab and his men marched all night and reached Hebron at daybreak. (2:32).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 31:11-13: The men of Jabesh-gilead take Saul's body down from Beth-shan and bury his bones under the tamarisk.
1 Samuel 16:1-13: Samuel anoints David at Bethlehem, the private anointing this public one begins to fulfil.
Genesis 32:1-2: Jacob names the place Mahanaim, two camps, when the angels of God meet him there.
Joshua 14:13-15: Hebron is given to Caleb for an inheritance, and the town becomes the chief city of the Judean hills.
2 Samuel 3:26-30: Joab takes Abner aside at the gate of Hebron and kills him for the blood of Asahel his brother.

translationNotes.note: Verse 13 has the two forces sit down facing each other on opposite sides of a pool. Gibeon is on the plateau about six miles north-west of Jerusalem, and James Pritchard excavated it in the 1950s, uncovering a great shaft cut down into the rock, about thirty-seven feet across and thirty-five deep, with a spiral stair running round the inside wall to the water. Water was the one thing both armies needed, and it belonged to neither of them.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶלְקַת הַצֻּרִים (Chelqat ha-Tsurim), the field of sword edges
translationNotes.note: Verses 14 to 16 propose a fight by champions, an equal number a side, to settle the matter without a general engagement; Goliath offers Israel the same arrangement at 1 Samuel 17:8-10. It works only if one side loses, and here every one of the twenty-four grabs his opposite number by the head and drives his sword into his side, so all of them fall together. The place keeps the name it earned, and the general battle begins anyway.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַחֲרֵי הַחֲנִית (acharei ha-chanit), the hinder end of the spear
translationNotes.note: Verse 23 has Abner kill Asahel with the back end of his spear, driven straight through him. A spear was shod at the rear with a metal spike so it could be planted upright in the ground, which is how Saul's stands beside his head while he sleeps (1 Samuel 26:7). Abner, running from a faster man, does not turn to face him; he thrusts backwards, and the blow that follows kills Asahel and starts a blood feud that runs through the next two chapters.

The main town of the southern hill country, about nineteen miles south of Jerusalem and 3,000 feet up, on good ground for flocks and vines. Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah there as a burial place (Genesis 23), and it was one of the six cities of refuge (Joshua 20:7). David rules Judah from Hebron for seven and a half years before taking Jerusalem.

stories.keyTakeaway: David consults the LORD, moves to Hebron, and is anointed king over Judah; meanwhile Abner installs Ish-Bosheth as king over the remaining tribes, leading to a fierce battle at Gibeon where David's forces prevail and Asahel is killed by Abner.

stories.title: ⚔️ 2 Samuel 3
summaryBullets: Now the war between the house of Saul and the house of David was protracted. And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker. (3:1).
And sons were born to David in Hebron: His firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel; (3:2).
his second was Chileab, by Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel; his third was Absalom, the son of Maacah daughter of King Talmai of Geshur; (3:3).
his fourth was Adonijah, the son of Haggith; his fifth was Shephatiah, the son of Abital; (3:4).
and his sixth was Ithream, by David’s wife Eglah. These sons were born to David in Hebron. (3:5).
During the war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner had continued to strengthen his position in the house of Saul. (3:6).
Now Saul had a concubine named Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. So Ish-bosheth questioned Abner, “Why did you sleep with my father’s concubine?” (3:7).

Abner was furious over Ish-bosheth’s accusation. “Am I the head of a dog that belongs to Judah?” he asked. “All this time I have been loyal to the house of your father Saul, to his brothers, and to his friends. I have not delivered you into the hand of David, but now you accuse me of wrongdoing with this woman! (3:8).
May God punish Abner, and ever so severely, if I do not do for David what the LORD has sworn to him: (3:9).
to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and to establish the throne of David over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.” (3:10).
And for fear of Abner, Ish-bosheth did not dare to say another word to him. (3:11).
Then Abner sent messengers on his behalf to say to David, “To whom does the land belong? Make your covenant with me, and surely my hand will be with you to bring all Israel over to you.” (3:12).
“Good,” replied David, “I will make a covenant with you. But there is one thing I require of you: Do not appear before me unless you bring Saul’s daughter Michal when you come to see me.” (3:13).
Then David sent messengers to say to Ish-bosheth son of Saul, “Give me back my wife, Michal, whom I betrothed to myself for a hundred Philistine foreskins.” (3:14).
So Ish-bosheth sent and took Michal from her husband Paltiel son of Laish. (3:15).
Her husband followed her, weeping all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, “Go back.” So he returned home. (3:16).
Now Abner conferred with the elders of Israel and said, “In the past you sought David as your king. (3:17).
Now take action, because the LORD has said to David, ‘Through My servant David I will save My people Israel from the hands of the Philistines and of all their enemies.’” (3:18).
Abner also spoke to the Benjamites. Then he went to Hebron to tell David all that seemed good to Israel and to the whole house of Benjamin. (3:19).
When Abner and twenty of his men came to David at Hebron, David held a feast for them. (3:20).

Then Abner said to David, “Let me go at once, and I will gather all Israel to my lord the king, that they may make a covenant with you, and that you may rule over all that your heart desires.” So David dismissed Abner, and he went in peace. (3:21).
Just then David’s soldiers and Joab returned from a raid, bringing with them a great plunder. But Abner was not with David in Hebron, because David had sent him on his way in peace. (3:22).
When Joab and all his troops arrived, he was informed, “Abner son of Ner came to see the king, who sent him on his way in peace.” (3:23).
So Joab went to the king and said, “What have you done? Look, Abner came to you. Why did you dismiss him? Now he is getting away! (3:24).
Surely you realize that Abner son of Ner came to deceive you and to track your movements and all that you are doing.” (3:25).
As soon as Joab had left David, he sent messengers after Abner, who brought him back from the well of Sirah. But David was unaware of it. (3:26).

When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab pulled him aside into the gateway, as if to speak to him privately, and there Joab stabbed him in the stomach. So Abner died on account of the blood of Joab’s brother Asahel. (3:27).
Afterward, David heard about this and said, “I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD concerning the blood of Abner son of Ner. (3:28).

May it whirl over the head of Joab and over the entire house of his father, and may the house of Joab never be without one having a discharge or skin disease, or one who leans on a staff or falls by the sword or lacks food.” (3:29).
(Joab and his brother Abishai murdered Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel in the battle at Gibeon.) (3:30).
Then David ordered Joab and all the people with him, “Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn before Abner.” And King David himself walked behind the funeral bier. (3:31).
When they buried Abner in Hebron, the king wept aloud at Abner’s tomb, and all the people wept. (3:32).
And the king sang this lament for Abner: “Should Abner die the death of a fool? (3:33).
Your hands were not bound, your feet were not fettered. As a man falls before the wicked, so also you fell.” And all the people wept over him even more. (3:34).

Then all the people came and urged David to eat something while it was still day, but David took an oath, saying, “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets!” (3:35).
All the people took note and were pleased. In fact, everything the king did pleased them. (3:36).
So on that day all the troops and all Israel were convinced that the king had no part in the murder of Abner son of Ner. (3:37).
Then the king said to his servants, “Do you not realize that a great prince has fallen today in Israel? (3:38).
And I am weak this day, though anointed as king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too fierce for me. May the LORD repay the evildoer according to his evil!” (3:39).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 19:4-13: The avenger of blood, and the difference the law draws between killing without intent and murder.
Numbers 35:16-25: The murderer is put to death, but the man who struck without enmity is sheltered until he is tried.
1 Samuel 18:20-27: Michal is given to David for a bride price of a hundred Philistines, and he brings two hundred.
1 Samuel 25:43-44: Saul gives Michal to Palti son of Laish while David is in exile.
1 Kings 2:5-6: David's charge to Solomon about Joab, who shed the blood of war in a time of peace.

translationNotes.note: Verses 2 to 5 list six sons by six different mothers, and the mothers are named because a prince's standing came through his mother's family. Two of these matter later. Amnon's mother is Ahinoam of Jezreel, and Absalom's is Maacah, daughter of the king of Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee; that foreign royal grandfather is where Absalom runs when he has killed Amnon and stays three years (13:37-38). The list is the seed of chapters 13 to 18.

David's demand in verse 14 rests on a payment: he had bought Michal from Saul with a hundred Philistine foreskins (1 Samuel 18:25-27), and Saul had then given her to another man. Recovering the previous king's daughter also strengthened his claim on the north, which is why the demand goes to Ish-bosheth rather than to the husband. Verse 16 records what that cost the husband, who follows her weeping as far as Bahurim and is told to go home.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֹּאֵל הַדָּם (goel ha-dam), the redeemer of blood
translationNotes.note: Verse 27 says plainly why Joab does it: Abner had killed his brother Asahel. The nearest male relative carried the duty of hunting down a killer, and there was no police force to do it instead. But Asahel died in open battle after being warned off twice, which the law counts differently from murder, and Hebron was one of the six cities of refuge set apart so a man in that position could stand trial rather than be cut down (Joshua 20:7). Joab takes him aside in the gateway as though to talk, and stabs him in the town where he should have been safe.

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

Ish-bosheth accuses Abner of going in to Saul's concubine Rizpah, and Abner's reaction is out of all proportion until you see what the charge means. Claiming a dead or displaced king's women was a claim on his throne, which is why Absalom does it publicly on the roof (2 Samuel 16:21-22) and why Solomon has Adonijah killed for asking for Abishag (1 Kings 2:22). It was a coup announced in the household.

stories.keyTakeaway: David's sons are born in Hebron while he grows stronger; Abner, angered by Ish-Bosheth's accusation about Saul's concubine, switches his allegiance to David and brokers peace, but Joab murders him in revenge for their brother Asahel, and David mourns publicly to prove his innocence.

stories.title: ⚔️ 2 Samuel 4
summaryBullets: Now when Ish-bosheth son of Saul heard that Abner had died in Hebron, he lost courage, and all Israel was dismayed. (4:1).

Saul’s son had two men who were leaders of raiding parties. One was named Baanah and the other Rechab; they were sons of Rimmon the Beerothite of the tribe of Benjamin— Beeroth is considered part of Benjamin, (4:2).
because the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have lived there as foreigners to this day. (4:3).

And Jonathan son of Saul had a son who was lame in his feet. He was five years old when the report about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel. His nurse picked him up and fled, but as she was hurrying to escape, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth. (4:4).
Now Rechab and Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, set out and arrived at the house of Ish-bosheth in the heat of the day, while the king was taking his midday nap. (4:5).
They entered the interior of the house as if to get some wheat, and they stabbed him in the stomach. Then Rechab and his brother Baanah slipped away. (4:6).
They had entered the house while Ish-bosheth was lying on his bed, and having stabbed and killed him, they beheaded him, took his head, and traveled all night by way of the Arabah. (4:7).

They brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron and said to the king, “Here is the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy who sought your life. Today the LORD has granted vengeance to my lord the king against Saul and his offspring.” (4:8).
But David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, “As surely as the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life from all distress, (4:9).
when someone told me, ‘Look, Saul is dead,’ and thought he was a bearer of good news, I seized him and put him to death at Ziklag. That was his reward for his news! (4:10).
How much more, when wicked men kill a righteous man in his own house and on his own bed, shall I not now require his blood from your hands and remove you from the earth!” (4:11).

So David commanded his young men, and they killed Rechab and Baanah. They cut off their hands and feet and hung their bodies by the pool in Hebron, but they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in Abner’s tomb in Hebron. (4:12).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 1:1-16: David executes the Amalekite who brought Saul's crown and claimed to have finished him off.
2 Samuel 9:1-13: Mephibosheth, the lame child introduced in verse 4, is later brought to eat at the king's table.
Deuteronomy 21:22-23: A body hanged on a tree must not remain overnight, for a hanged man is cursed by God.
Genesis 9:5-6: From every man I will require a reckoning for the life of his brother; whoever sheds man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed.
2 Samuel 2:8-9: Abner sets Ish-bosheth over Gilead, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel from Mahanaim.

translationNotes.note: The name in this book means man of shame. The same son of Saul is called Esh-baal, man of Baal, in the family list at 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:39, and Jonathan's son Mephibosheth appears there as Merib-baal (1 Chronicles 8:34). Baal means lord or master and was the name of the Canaanite storm god, and the element was replaced with bosheth, shame, in these names.

Beeroth was one of the four towns of the Gibeonites, the people who obtained a treaty from Joshua by pretending to have come from far away and who were spared and made woodcutters and water carriers (Joshua 9:3-27, with the towns listed in 9:17). Verse 3 notes that the Beerothites had fled to Gittaim and were living there as resident aliens. 2 Samuel 21:1-2 records that Saul had tried to wipe the Gibeonites out.

A town in the dry Negev in the south that Achish king of Gath handed to David when David was living as a Philistine vassal, sixteen months in all (1 Samuel 27:5-7). Amalekite raiders burned it and carried off the families while David was away (1 Samuel 30:1-2). It is where the Amalekite came in with Saul's crown and armlet and was executed for saying he had finished Saul off (2 Samuel 1:1-16), which is the case David cites in verse 10.

translationNotes.term: Require his blood from your hands
translationNotes.note: Shed blood was held to defile the land itself until it was answered for. Genesis 9:5-6 states the requirement, and Numbers 35:31-33 forbids accepting any ransom for a murderer and says no atonement can be made for the land except by the blood of the man who shed blood. David is not taking personal revenge; he is discharging a legal obligation on the man whose house the killing happened in.

translationNotes.term: Cut off their hands and feet and hung their bodies
translationNotes.note: Mutilating and displaying a corpse in a public place, here beside the pool at Hebron, was punishment aimed at everyone who walked past. The Philistines had done the same to Saul, fastening his body to the wall at Beth-shan (1 Samuel 31:10). Israel's own law limits the practice: a body hung on a tree must be taken down and buried the same day, because a hanged man is under God's curse and the land must not be defiled (Deuteronomy 21:22-23).

stories.keyTakeaway: Rekab and Baanah assassinate Ish-Bosheth in his bed and bring his head to David, expecting reward; David executes them instead, viewing their act as murder of an innocent man rather than a service to him.

headings.text: The Execution of Rechab and Baanah

stories.title: 🏛️ 2 Samuel 5
summaryBullets: Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, “Here we are, your own flesh and blood. (5:1).

Even in times past, while Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them back. And to you the LORD said, ‘You will shepherd My people Israel, and you will be ruler over them.’” (5:2).
So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, where King David made with them a covenant before the LORD. And they anointed him king over Israel. (5:3).
David was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned forty years. (5:4).
In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah. (5:5).

Now the king and his men marched to Jerusalem against the Jebusites who inhabited the land. The Jebusites said to David: “You will never get in here. Even the blind and lame can repel you.” For they thought, “David cannot get in here.” (5:6).
Nevertheless , David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David). (5:7).

On that day he said, “Whoever attacks the Jebusites must use the water shaft to reach the lame and blind who are despised by David.” That is why it is said, “The blind and the lame will never enter the palace.” (5:8).
So David took up residence in the fortress and called it the City of David. He built it up all the way around, from the supporting terraces inward. (5:9).
And David became greater and greater, for the LORD God of Hosts was with him. (5:10).
Now Hiram king of Tyre sent envoys to David, along with cedar logs, carpenters, and stonemasons, and they built a palace for David. (5:11).
And David realized that the LORD had established him as king over Israel and had exalted his kingdom for the sake of His people Israel. (5:12).
After he had arrived from Hebron, David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to him. (5:13).
These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, (5:14).
Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, (5:15).
Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet. (5:16).
When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, they all went in search of him; but David learned of this and went down to the stronghold. (5:17).
Now the Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim. (5:18).

So David inquired of the LORD, “Should I go up against the Philistines? Will You deliver them into my hand?” “Go up,” replied the LORD, “for I will surely deliver the Philistines into your hand.” (5:19).
So David went to Baal-perazim, where he defeated the Philistines and said, “Like a bursting flood, the LORD has burst out against my enemies before me.” So he called that place Baal-perazim. (5:20).
There the Philistines abandoned their idols, and David and his men carried them away. (5:21).
Once again the Philistines came up and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim. (5:22).
So David inquired of the LORD, who answered, “Do not march straight up, but circle around behind them and attack them in front of the balsam trees. (5:23).
As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move quickly, because this will mean that the LORD has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines.” (5:24).
So David did as the LORD had commanded him, and he struck down the Philistines all the way from Gibeon to Gezer. (5:25).
crossRefs: 1 Chronicles 11:1-9: The parallel account of the anointing at Hebron and the capture of the stronghold of Zion.
Joshua 15:63: Judah could not drive out the Jebusites, who went on living in Jerusalem alongside them.
Judges 1:21: Benjamin did not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem either, and they remained there.
1 Chronicles 14:8-17: The parallel account of the two Philistine battles and the sound of marching in the treetops.
Genesis 49:10: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet.

translationNotes.note: Verse 7 uses the name for one thing only: the Jebusite fortress on the southern spur of the ridge, which David takes and renames the City of David. It is a small place, roughly eleven acres, on a steep-sided finger of rock between two valleys. From there the name spreads outward in Scripture, first to the temple hill just north of it, then to Jerusalem as a whole, and then in the prophets to the people of God themselves. Every later use of Zion starts from this captured stronghold.

Verse 9 says David built the city round about from the Millo inward, and English versions render the word as supporting terraces because that is what it was. The name comes from the verb to fill, and it means a built-up stepped fill of stone and earth on the steep eastern slope, holding back the hillside so that buildings could stand on ground that was otherwise too sharp to use. Solomon repairs and extends it (1 Kings 9:15, 11:27) and Hezekiah strengthens it again (2 Chronicles 32:5).

translationNotes.term: Hiram of Tyre and the cedar
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַרְזֵי אֲרָזִים (arze arazim), cedar logs
translationNotes.note: Tyre was a Phoenician port built on an island off the coast north of Carmel, rich on sea trade and on the timber of the Lebanon range behind it. Verse 11 has its king send cedar logs and both carpenters and stonemasons, because Israel had neither. Cedar was the prestige building timber of the ancient world, straight-grained, huge, fragrant and resistant to rot, and the highland oak and terebinth of Judah could not match it. The same arrangement supplies Solomon's temple a generation later (1 Kings 5:1-12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵמֶק רְפָאִים (Emeq Refaim) - בַּעַל פְּרָצִים (Baal Peratsim), master of breakings-through
translationNotes.note: Verses 18 and 22 have the Philistines spread out in this valley twice. It is the broad, level basin running south-west out of Jerusalem toward Bethlehem, good grain land (Isaiah 17:5) and the natural approach to the city from Philistine country, which is why they use it and why the new capital had to be defended there first. David names the site of the first victory Baal-perazim, which means master of breakings-through, from the phrase he uses in verse 20 about water bursting a dam.

Verse 8 has David offer command to whoever gets up the tsinnor into the city. Jerusalem's only water was the Gihon spring outside the wall in the valley, and the city was tunnelled and shafted so people could reach it under cover. Charles Warren mapped a shaft and tunnel system running from the spring up inside the ridge in 1867. A fortress that cannot be starved out can still be entered through the pipe that keeps it alive.

stories.keyTakeaway: All the tribes of Israel anoint David as king at Hebron; he captures Jerusalem from the Jebusites, takes up residence there, and defeats the Philistines in two battles after consulting the Lord.

headings.text: David Anointed King of All Israel

stories.title: 🏛️ 2 Samuel 6
summaryBullets: David again assembled the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand in all. (6:1).

And he and all his troops set out for Baale of Judah to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the Name— the name of the LORD of Hosts, who is enthroned between the cherubim that are on it. (6:2).
They set the ark of God on a new cart and brought it from the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were guiding the new cart, (6:3).
bringing with it the ark of God. And Ahio was walking in front of the ark. (6:4).
David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD with all kinds of wood instruments, harps, stringed instruments, tambourines, sistrums, and cymbals. (6:5).
When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark of God, because the oxen had stumbled. (6:6).
And the anger of the LORD burned against Uzzah, and God struck him down on the spot for his irreverence, and he died there beside the ark of God. (6:7).
Then David became angry because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah. So he named that place Perez-uzzah, as it is called to this day. (6:8).
That day David feared the LORD and asked, “How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?” (6:9).
So he was unwilling to move the ark of the LORD to the City of David; instead, he took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. (6:10).
Thus the ark of the LORD remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and the LORD blessed him and all his household. (6:11).

Now it was reported to King David, “The LORD has blessed the house of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God.” So David went and had the ark of God brought up from the house of Obed-edom into the City of David with rejoicing. (6:12).
When those carrying the ark of the LORD had advanced six paces, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened calf. (6:13).
And David, wearing a linen ephod, danced with all his might before the LORD, (6:14).
while he and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and the sounding of the ram’s horn. (6:15).

As the ark of the LORD was entering the City of David, Saul’s daughter Michal looked down from a window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart. (6:16).
So they brought the ark of the LORD and set it in its place inside the tent that David had pitched for it. Then David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD. (6:17).
When David had finished sacrificing the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of Hosts. (6:18).
Then he distributed to every man and woman among the multitude of Israel a loaf of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake. And all the people departed, each to his own home. (6:19).

When David returned home to bless his own household, Saul’s daughter Michal came out to meet him. “How the king of Israel has distinguished himself today!” she said. “He has uncovered himself today in the sight of the maidservants of his subjects, like a vulgar person would do.” (6:20).

But David said to Michal, “I was dancing before the LORD, who chose me over your father and all his house when He appointed me ruler over the LORD’s people Israel. I will celebrate before the LORD, (6:21).
and I will humiliate and humble myself even more than this. Yet I will be honored by the maidservants of whom you have spoken.” (6:22).
And Michal the daughter of Saul had no children to the day of her death. (6:23).
crossRefs: 1 Chronicles 13:1-14: The parallel account of the first attempt to move the ark and the death of Uzzah.
1 Chronicles 15:1-29: David's second attempt, carried out by Levites bearing the ark on poles as the law required.
Numbers 4:15: The Kohathites carry the holy things after Aaron has covered them, and must not touch them, or they die.
Exodus 25:12-15: The poles are set into the ark's rings and are never to be taken out of them.
1 Samuel 6:19: The men of Beth-shemesh are struck down for looking into the ark of the LORD.

translationNotes.note: A chest of acacia wood overlaid inside and out with gold, about three and three-quarter feet long and two and a quarter wide and high, holding the two stone tablets, with a solid gold lid and two cherubim of hammered gold facing each other above it (Exodus 25:10-22). Four gold rings held two carrying poles that were never to be taken out, and Numbers 4:15 and 7:9 make it plain that the sons of Kohath carried it on their shoulders and were not to touch the thing itself on pain of death. Everything that goes wrong in this chapter follows from that instruction being ignored.

The ark was built with rings and two poles that were never to be removed, so that Levites carried it on their shoulders and nobody's hand touched it (Exodus 25:12-15, Numbers 7:9). A cart is how the Philistines had shipped it back (1 Samuel 6:7). When the oxen stumbled, Uzzah put out his hand, and 1 Chronicles 15:13 gives David's own verdict afterward: they had not sought God about the proper way.

On the second attempt, verse 13 has an ox and a fattened animal offered once the bearers had gone six steps. This was not a sacrifice every six paces the whole nine miles; it marks the start of the procession, with the offering made as soon as it was clear the carriers were not struck down. The distance from Obed-edom's house to Jerusalem was covered with singing, trumpets, and dancing the rest of the way.

translationNotes.term: A loaf, a date cake and a raisin cake
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶשְׁפָּר (eshpar) - אֲשִׁישָׁה (ashishah), a pressed cake
translationNotes.note: Verse 19 has David hand out a portion to every man and woman in the crowd before sending them home. This is the shared meal of a peace offering: part burned, part given to the priest, and the rest eaten by the worshippers on the spot (Leviticus 7:15-16). Pressed cakes of dates and raisins were the standard festival ration because they kept and travelled, which is why they turn up in Abigail's provision train (1 Samuel 25:18) and again at 1 Chronicles 12:40. A king feeding the whole assembly at his own cost is the public half of the event.

A flat, hard, outdoor surface, usually a leveled rock or beaten-earth circle at the edge of town, where harvested grain was separated from chaff. Oxen pulled a wooden sledge over the stalks; the mixed kernels and chaff were then winnowed in the wind. Threshing floors doubled as public civic spaces (Ruth 3; 2 Samuel 24:18; Solomon's temple site).

stories.keyTakeaway: David attempts to move the ark of God to Jerusalem with thirty thousand men, but Uzzah is struck dead when he touches it; David later brings the ark successfully to the city with celebration and sacrifice, then rebukes his wife Michal for mocking his dancing before the LORD.

stories.title: 🏛️ 2 Samuel 7
summaryBullets: After the king had settled into his palace and the LORD had given him rest from all his enemies around him, (7:1).
he said to Nathan the prophet, “Here I am, living in a house of cedar, while the ark of God remains in a tent.” (7:2).
And Nathan replied to the king, “Go and do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you.” (7:3).
But that night the word of the LORD came to Nathan, saying, (7:4).
“Go and tell My servant David that this is what the LORD says: Are you the one to build for Me a house to dwell in? (7:5).
For I have not dwelt in a house from the day I brought the Israelites up out of Egypt until this day, but I have moved about with a tent as My dwelling. (7:6).
In all My journeys with all the Israelites, have I ever asked any of the leaders I appointed to shepherd My people Israel, ‘Why haven’t you built Me a house of cedar?’ (7:7).
Now then, you are to tell My servant David that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be the ruler over My people Israel. (7:8).
I have been with you wherever you have gone, and I have cut off all your enemies from before you. Now I will make for you a name like that of the greatest in the land. (7:9).

And I will provide a place for My people Israel and will plant them so that they may dwell in a place of their own and be disturbed no more. No longer will the sons of wickedness oppress them as they did at the beginning (7:10).
and have done since the day I appointed judges over My people Israel. I will give you rest from all your enemies. The LORD declares to you that He Himself will establish a house for you. (7:11).
And when your days are fulfilled and you rest with your fathers, I will raise up your descendant after you, who will come from your own body, and I will establish his kingdom. (7:12).
He will build a house for My Name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. (7:13).
I will be his Father, and he will be My son. When he does wrong, I will discipline him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men. (7:14).
But My loving devotion will never be removed from him as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before you. (7:15).
Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever.” (7:16).
So Nathan relayed to David all the words of this entire revelation. (7:17).
Then King David went in, sat before the LORD, and said, “Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far? (7:18).
And as if this was a small thing in Your eyes, O Lord GOD, You have also spoken about the future of the house of Your servant. Is this Your custom with man, O Lord GOD? (7:19).
What more can David say to You? For You know Your servant, O Lord GOD. (7:20).
For the sake of Your word and according to Your own heart, You have accomplished this great thing and revealed it to Your servant. (7:21).
How great You are, O Lord GOD! For there is none like You, and there is no God but You, according to everything we have heard with our own ears. (7:22).

And who is like Your people Israel — the one nation on earth whom God went out to redeem as a people for Himself and to make a name for Himself? You performed great and awesome wonders by driving out nations and their gods from before Your people, whom You redeemed for Yourself from Egypt. (7:23).
For You have established Your people Israel as Your very own forever, and You, O LORD, have become their God. (7:24).
And now, O LORD God, confirm forever the word You have spoken concerning Your servant and his house. Do as You have promised, (7:25).
so that Your name will be magnified forever when it is said, ‘The LORD of Hosts is God over Israel.’ And the house of Your servant David will be established before You. (7:26).

For You, O LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, have revealed this to Your servant when You said, ‘I will build a house for you.’ Therefore Your servant has found the courage to offer this prayer to You. (7:27).
And now, O Lord GOD, You are God! Your words are true, and You have promised this goodness to Your servant. (7:28).

Now therefore, may it please You to bless the house of Your servant, that it may continue forever before You. For You, O Lord GOD, have spoken, and with Your blessing the house of Your servant will be blessed forever.” (7:29).
crossRefs: 1 Chronicles 17:1-27: The parallel account of the same night, the same word through Nathan, and the same prayer.
Psalm 89:19-37: The covenant sworn to David, that his offspring will endure forever and his throne as the days of heaven.
Psalm 132:11-12: The LORD swore to David a sure oath: one of the sons of your body I will set on your throne.
Luke 1:32-33: He will be given the throne of His father David, and of His kingdom there will be no end.
Acts 2:29-31: David, being a prophet, knew that God had sworn to set one of his descendants on his throne.

translationNotes.note: The chapter turns on one word used three ways. In verse 2 David lives in a house of cedar, a building. In verse 5 he proposes to build God a house, a temple. In verses 11 and 16 God answers that He will build David a house, meaning a family line that continues on the throne. Hebrew uses bayit for all three, so the exchange is a play the English cannot carry in a single word, and the third sense is the one the rest of Scripture picks up.

Nathan holds a standing position at court, and the chapter shows exactly what that meant. In verse 3 he gives David his own opinion, go and do it, and that night he is sent back with a word that reverses him, which he delivers in full. He turns up twice more at the sharpest moments in the book and the next: to confront David over Uriah (12:1-14), and to secure Solomon's succession against Adonijah (1 Kings 1:11-27). Gad, called David's seer, holds the same kind of post (24:11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יְרִיעָה (yeriah), a curtain or tent-cloth
translationNotes.note: Verses 2 and 6 set a cedar palace against a tent of curtains. The tabernacle was a portable frame hung with woven panels and covered with skins, designed to be struck and carried (Exodus 26), and it had housed the ark since the exodus; from Joshua 18:1 it had stood at Shiloh, and at this point the ark sits in a tent David has pitched in Jerusalem (6:17). Verse 6 has God point out that He has never asked for anything else.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַד־עוֹלָם (ad olam), to the age
translationNotes.note: The promise in verses 13 and 16 is unconditional in a way the covenant at Sinai was not: the throne, the kingdom and the house are established ad olam, without a term set. Verse 14 adds that when the son does wrong he will be disciplined with the rod of men, and verse 15 that God's steadfast love will not be taken from him as it was taken from Saul. The psalms return to this promise directly (Psalm 89:3-4, 132:11), and both Gospel genealogies open by naming Jesus the son of David (Matthew 1:1, Luke 1:32-33).

stories.keyTakeaway: David proposes building a house for the ark of God, but Nathan delivers a message from the LORD saying David's son will build it instead and God will establish David's dynasty forever. David responds by sitting before the LORD and praying a prayer of thanksgiving and petition for God to fulfill this promise concerning his house.

stories.title: 🛡️ 2 Samuel 8
summaryBullets: Some time later, David defeated the Philistines, subdued them, and took Metheg-ammah from the hand of the Philistines. (8:1).

David also defeated the Moabites, made them lie down on the ground, and measured them off with a cord. He measured off with two lengths those to be put to death, and with one length those to be spared. So the Moabites became subject to David and brought him tribute. (8:2).
David also defeated Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, who had marched out to restore his dominion along the Euphrates River. (8:3).
David captured from him a thousand chariots, seven thousand charioteers, and twenty thousand foot soldiers, and he hamstrung all the horses except a hundred he kept for the chariots. (8:4).
When the Arameans of Damascus came to help King Hadadezer of Zobah, David struck down twenty-two thousand of their men. (8:5).
Then he placed garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became subject to David and brought him tribute. So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went. (8:6).
And David took the gold shields that belonged to the officers of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem. (8:7).
And from Betah and Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, King David took a large amount of bronze. (8:8).
When King Toi of Hamath heard that David had defeated the entire army of Hadadezer, (8:9).
he sent his son Joram to greet King David and bless him for fighting and defeating Hadadezer, who had been at war with Toi. Joram brought with him articles of silver and gold and bronze, (8:10).
and King David dedicated these to the LORD, along with the silver and gold he had dedicated from all the nations he had subdued— (8:11).
from Edom and Moab, from the Ammonites and Philistines and Amalekites, and from the spoil of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah. (8:12).
And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. (8:13).
He placed garrisons throughout Edom, and all the Edomites were subject to David. So the LORD made David victorious wherever he went. (8:14).
Thus David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people: (8:15).
Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder; (8:16).
Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests; Seraiah was the scribe; (8:17).
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites; and David’s sons were priestly leaders. (8:18).
crossRefs: 1 Chronicles 18:1-17: The parallel account of the same campaigns, the same tribute, and the same list of officials.
Deuteronomy 17:16: The king shall not multiply horses for himself, nor cause the people to return to Egypt to get them.
Joshua 11:6,9: Joshua hamstrings the horses of the northern kings and burns their chariots with fire.
Numbers 24:17-18: A star shall come out of Jacob, and Edom shall become a possession.
1 Kings 7:45-47: Solomon's bronze vessels, made from bronze in such quantity that its weight was never determined.

translationNotes.note: Verse 2 reports the fate of the Moabite prisoners without a word of comment. They were made to lie down on the ground in a row and measured off with a cord: two cord-lengths of men put to death, one cord-length spared. It is selection by proportion, roughly two in three killed, carried out on men already taken. The text states it and moves straight on to the tribute they paid afterwards.

translationNotes.term: The recorder and the court list
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַזְכִּיר (mazkir), the one who reminds
translationNotes.note: Verses 15 to 18 are the first list of a working Israelite government, and two of the titles need unpacking. The mazkir, rendered recorder, comes from the verb to remember: he kept the royal annals and controlled what came before the king, closer to a chief of staff than to a clerk. Alongside him sit the commander of the army, two priests, the scribe, and the commander of the guard. The same list appears again after the rebellions, with one post added, an officer over the forced labour (20:23-26).

Verse 18 puts Benaiah over David's personal guard, and they are foreigners. The Cherethites are linked with the Philistine coast wherever else they appear (1 Samuel 30:14, Ezekiel 25:16, Zephaniah 2:5), so this is a corps of professional soldiers from outside Israel, paid by and loyal to the king rather than to any tribe. That is precisely why they are worth having: when Absalom takes the country, the Cherethites and Pelethites walk out of Jerusalem with David (15:18), and they are still with him at Solomon's coronation (1 Kings 1:38).

Originally professional copyists of Scripture. By the New Testament era, scholar-teachers of the Law; often, though not exclusively, aligned with the Pharisees. They formed the educated religious class that adjudicated everyday halakhic questions.

Verse 4 has David keep a hundred chariot teams and cripple the rest by cutting the tendon at the back of the hock, so the animal could never pull again. Chariots were the most expensive weapon of the age and needed flat ground, trained pairs, wheelwrights, and roads, none of which Israel's hill country had. Cutting the horses denied the technology to the enemy without Israel taking it up.

stories.keyTakeaway: David defeats the Philistines, Moabites, Hadadezer of Zobah, the Arameans, and the Edomites in a series of military campaigns; he dedicates the plunder to the Lord and establishes garrisons throughout the conquered territories. His officials and military commanders are listed, and the Lord grants him victory wherever he goes.

stories.title: 🛡️ 2 Samuel 9
summaryBullets: Then David asked, “Is there anyone left from the house of Saul to whom I can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan?” (9:1).
And there was a servant of the house of Saul named Ziba. They summoned him to David, and the king inquired, “Are you Ziba?” “I am your servant,” he replied. (9:2).
So the king asked, “Is there anyone left of the house of Saul to whom I can show the kindness of God?” Ziba answered, “There is still Jonathan’s son, who is lame in both feet.” (9:3).
“Where is he?” replied the king. And Ziba said, “Indeed, he is in Lo-debar at the house of Machir son of Ammiel.” (9:4).
So King David had him brought from the house of Machir son of Ammiel in Lo-debar. (9:5).
And when Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David, he fell facedown in reverence. Then David said, “Mephibosheth!” “I am your servant,” he replied. (9:6).

“Do not be afraid,” said David, “for surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore to you all the land of your grandfather Saul, and you will always eat at my table.” (9:7).
Mephibosheth bowed down and said, “What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog like me?” (9:8).
Then the king summoned Saul’s servant Ziba and said to him, “I have given to your master’s grandson all that belonged to Saul and to all his house. (9:9).

You and your sons and servants are to work the ground for him and bring in the harvest, so that your master’s grandson may have food to eat. But Mephibosheth, your master’s grandson, is always to eat at my table.” Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants. (9:10).
And Ziba said to the king, “Your servant will do all that my lord the king has commanded.” So Mephibosheth ate at David’s table like one of the king’s own sons. (9:11).
And Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica, and all who dwelt in the house of Ziba were servants of Mephibosheth. (9:12).
So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king’s table, and he was lame in both feet. (9:13).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 20:14-17: Jonathan makes David swear never to cut off his covenant kindness from his house.
1 Samuel 20:42: The LORD is between me and you, and between my offspring and yours, forever.
2 Samuel 4:4: Jonathan's son is dropped by his nurse at five years old on the day the news came from Jezreel, and is left lame.
2 Samuel 16:1-4: Ziba meets David with supplies and accuses Mephibosheth of staying in Jerusalem to claim the throne.
2 Samuel 21:7: David spares Mephibosheth from the Gibeonites because of the oath sworn between him and Jonathan.

translationNotes.note: Chesed is loyalty owed under a standing obligation and kept after the obligation could safely be dropped. Verse 1 asks whether anyone of Saul's house is left, so that David may show chesed for Jonathan's sake, and verse 3 calls it the chesed of God. This is not a spontaneous kindness; it is a clause being honoured. Jonathan had made David swear it, for himself and for his descendants, at 1 Samuel 20:14-15, at a time when the odds ran the other way.

4:4 explains the injury: Mephibosheth was five years old when the news came from Jezreel, his nurse picked him up and ran, and he fell and was crippled in both feet. In a world with no wheelchairs, a man lame in both feet could not farm, could not fight and could not travel, so he depended entirely on a household that would keep him. Verse 13 notes that he lived in Jerusalem and ate at the king's table, and repeats that he was lame in both feet, which is why that arrangement was the whole of his security.

Verse 4 finds the last heir of Saul's house living at Lo-debar in Gilead, east of the Jordan, in the household of Machir son of Ammiel. Across the river was the safest place to keep him: outside the reach of the new king, in the region that had backed Ish-bosheth. Machir turns up once more, sending food and bedding to David at Mahanaim when Absalom drives him out (17:27-29), so the man sheltering Saul's grandson later supplies David's army.

Verses 7, 10, 11, and 13 repeat that Mephibosheth eats at the king's table. A place at the table was a formal grant of maintenance for life at royal expense, recorded the same way for the released Jehoiachin in Babylon (2 Kings 25:29). It also kept the last heir of the previous dynasty where the king could see him every day.

stories.keyTakeaway: David seeks out anyone remaining from Saul's house to show kindness for Jonathan's sake and brings Mephibosheth, Jonathan's lame son, from hiding to restore his family's land and grant him a permanent place at the royal table.

stories.title: 🛡️ 2 Samuel 10
summaryBullets: Some time later, the king of the Ammonites died and was succeeded by his son Hanun. (10:1).

And David said, “I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me.” So David sent some of his servants to console Hanun concerning his father. But when they arrived in the land of the Ammonites, (10:2).

the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord, “Just because David has sent you comforters, do you really believe he is showing respect for your father? Has not David instead sent his servants to explore the city, spy it out, and overthrow it?” (10:3).
So Hanun took David’s servants, shaved off half of each man’s beard, cut off their garments at the hips, and sent them away. (10:4).

When this was reported to David, he sent messengers to meet the men, since they had been thoroughly humiliated. The king told them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards have grown back, and then return.” (10:5).

When the Ammonites realized that they had become a stench to David, they hired twenty thousand Aramean foot soldiers from Beth-rehob and Zoba, as well as a thousand men from the king of Maacah and twelve thousand men from Tob. (10:6).
On hearing this, David sent Joab and the entire army of mighty men. (10:7).

The Ammonites marched out and arrayed themselves for battle at the entrance of the city gate, while the Arameans of Zobah and Rehob and the men of Tob and Maacah were by themselves in the open country. (10:8).
When Joab saw the battle lines before him and behind him, he selected some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Arameans. (10:9).
And he placed the rest of the troops under the command of his brother Abishai, who arrayed them against the Ammonites. (10:10).
“If the Arameans are too strong for me,” said Joab, “then you will come to my rescue. And if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come to your rescue. (10:11).
Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God. May the LORD do what is good in His sight.” (10:12).
So Joab and his troops advanced to fight the Arameans, who fled before him. (10:13).
When the Ammonites saw that the Arameans had fled, they too fled before Abishai, and they entered the city. So Joab returned from fighting against the Ammonites and came to Jerusalem. (10:14).
When the Arameans saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they regrouped. (10:15).
Hadadezer sent messengers to bring more Arameans from beyond the Euphrates, and they came to Helam with Shobach the commander of Hadadezer’s army leading them. (10:16).
When this was reported to David, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and went to Helam. Then the Arameans arrayed themselves against David and fought against him. (10:17).
But the Arameans fled before Israel, and David killed seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers. He also struck down Shobach the commander of their army, who died there. (10:18).

When all the kings who were subject to Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and became subject to them. So the Arameans were afraid to help the Ammonites anymore. (10:19).
crossRefs: 1 Chronicles 19:1-19: The parallel account of the same insult, the same battle, and the same Aramean surrender.
1 Samuel 11:1-11: Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and demands the right eye of every man in it.
Genesis 19:36-38: Lot's younger daughter bears Ben-ammi, the father of the Ammonites.
Leviticus 19:27: Israel is forbidden to round off the hair at the temples or to mar the edges of the beard.
Isaiah 20:4: Captives are led away naked and barefoot with buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt.

translationNotes.note: Two mutilations in verse 4, and both were meant to be seen. A full beard was a grown man's dignity, and Leviticus 19:27 forbids marring its edges; shaving off half of each man's beard left a disfigurement that could not be hidden and took months to grow out. Cutting their robes off at the hips exposed them, which is the same shaming Assyria is said to inflict on prisoners at Isaiah 20:4. They are ambassadors, so the insult is aimed at the king who sent them, and verse 5 has David keep them at Jericho until their beards grow back.

Verses 6 and 8 name four Aramean states hired for the war: Beth-rehob and Zobah in the Beqaa valley of modern Lebanon, Maacah at the foot of Mount Hermon, and Tob east of Gilead, where Jephthah had gone when his brothers drove him out (Judges 11:3). Aram is the country and people English calls Syria, north and north-east of Israel, and Zobah was the strongest of these kingdoms before Damascus rose. They are Israel's northern neighbours for the next three centuries.

Verse 6 has Ammon hire thirty-three thousand foreign troops rather than field its own, and 1 Chronicles 19:6 gives the price: a thousand talents of silver, roughly thirty-seven tons of it, for chariots and horsemen. Buying an army was normal practice for a small state with money and not enough men, and it is what makes this a regional war instead of a border quarrel. The whole thing starts with an insult to a delegation of condolence.

Verses 9 to 11 describe Joab caught between two forces, the Ammonites drawn up at the city gate in front and the hired Arameans in the open country behind him. He splits his army, takes the picked men against the Arameans himself, gives the rest to Abishai against the Ammonites, and they agree that whichever of them is too strong for his enemy will come to the other's help. That is a stated plan for fighting in two directions at once, and verse 12 is the order that goes with it.

stories.keyTakeaway: David sends envoys to console the new Ammonite king, but Hanun humiliates them; the Ammonites hire Aramean allies and are defeated by Joab, then a larger Aramean force regrouping under Hadadezer is routed by David, leaving the Arameans unwilling to support Ammon further.

stories.title: 🔥 2 Samuel 11
summaryBullets: In the spring, at the time when kings march out to war, David sent out Joab and his servants with the whole army of Israel. They destroyed the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah, but David remained in Jerusalem. (11:1).
One evening David got up from his bed and strolled around on the roof of the palace. And from the roof he saw a woman bathing— a very beautiful woman. (11:2).
So David sent and inquired about the woman, and he was told, “This is Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite.” (11:3).
Then David sent messengers to get her, and when she came to him, he slept with her. (Now she had just purified herself from her uncleanness.) Then she returned home. (11:4).
And the woman conceived and sent word to David, saying, “I am pregnant.” (11:5).
At this, David sent orders to Joab: “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” So Joab sent him to David. (11:6).
When Uriah came to him, David asked how Joab and the troops were doing and how the war was going. (11:7).
Then he said to Uriah, “Go down to your house and wash your feet.” So Uriah left the palace, and a gift from the king followed him. (11:8).
But Uriah slept at the door of the palace with all his master’s servants; he did not go down to his house. (11:9).
And David was told, “Uriah did not go home.” “Haven’t you just arrived from a journey?” David asked Uriah. “Why didn’t you go home?” (11:10).

Uriah answered, “The ark and Israel and Judah are dwelling in tents, and my master Joab and his soldiers are camped in the open field. How can I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? As surely as you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do such a thing!” (11:11).
“Stay here one more day,” David said to Uriah, “and tomorrow I will send you back.” So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next. (11:12).
Then David invited Uriah to eat and drink with him, and he got Uriah drunk. And in the evening Uriah went out to lie down on his cot with his master’s servants, but he did not go home. (11:13).
The next morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it with Uriah. (11:14).
In the letter he wrote: “Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed.” (11:15).
So as Joab besieged the city, he assigned Uriah to a place where he knew the strongest enemy soldiers were. (11:16).
And when the men of the city came out and fought against Joab, some of David’s servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite also died. (11:17).
Joab sent to David a full account of the battle (11:18).
and instructed the messenger, “When you have finished giving the king a full account of the battle, (11:19).
if the king’s anger flares, he may ask you, ‘Why did you get so close to the city to fight? Did you not realize they would shoot from atop the wall? (11:20).

Who struck Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth? Was it not a woman who dropped an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died in Thebez? Why did you get so close to the wall?’ If he asks you this, then you are to say, ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well.’” (11:21).
So the messenger set out and reported to David all that Joab had sent him to say. (11:22).
The messenger said to David, “The men overpowered us and came out against us in the field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate. (11:23).
Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall, and some of the king’s servants were killed. And your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well.” (11:24).

Then David told the messenger, “Say this to Joab: ‘Do not let this matter upset you, for the sword devours one as well as another. Strengthen your attack against the city and demolish it.’ Encourage him with these words.” (11:25).
When Uriah’s wife heard that her husband was dead, she mourned for him. (11:26).
And when the time of mourning was over, David had her brought to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD. (11:27).
crossRefs: Exodus 20:13-14,17: You shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not covet your neighbour's wife.
Leviticus 20:10: If a man commits adultery with the wife of his neighbour, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall be put to death.
Deuteronomy 17:17: The king shall not multiply wives for himself, or his heart will turn away.
Leviticus 15:19-24: A woman is unclean seven days at her period and washes afterward, the purification noted in verse 4.
2 Samuel 23:39: Uriah the Hittite is listed by name as the last of David's thirty mighty men.

translationNotes.note: The parenthesis in verse 4 looks like a stray detail and is doing hard work. Leviticus 15:19-30 sets seven days of ritual separation for a woman's monthly period, ending with washing, so the note tells the reader she had just finished her period. That establishes two things at once: she was not already pregnant, and the child announced in verse 5 can only be David's. The whole plot of the chapter rests on that one clause.

The order in verse 8 is an idiom, not hygiene advice. Washing the feet was the first thing done on arriving home or at a host's house after a day on dusty roads (Genesis 18:4, 19:2, Luke 7:44), so go down to your house and wash your feet means settle in for the night and resume your ordinary life with your wife. Uriah understands it perfectly, which is why his answer in verse 11 refuses exactly that, and why he sleeps at the palace door instead.

Verses 14 and 15 turn on the physical facts of writing. A letter was written on a sheet, folded, tied and sealed with clay stamped by the sender's own seal, so that any tampering showed. Reading and writing were the trade of a small class of scribes, and the carrier was neither expected nor able to open it. David hands Uriah the order for his own death and sends him back to the siege with it, and Joab reads it as an instruction from the commander in chief.

translationNotes.term: The time when kings go out
translationNotes.note: Verse 1 dates this at the turn of the year, the campaign season. Armies moved once the winter rains stopped and the roads dried, roughly from March, and once the barley and wheat were in so troops could live off the land. Fighting stopped again with the autumn rains. The verse says twice what David was not doing while the season ran.

Israelite roofs were flat, reached by an outside stair, and used for sleeping in the heat, drying grain and figs, and working. Deuteronomy 22:8 requires a parapet on a new house because people lived up there. The palace stood high on the ridge above the houses of the old city, so a man walking his roof looked down into the courtyards below.

The Hittites ran an empire out of Anatolia, in modern Turkey, and their people turn up all through Scripture from Abraham's dealings at Hebron onward. For a long time the Bible was the main record of them, until the Hittite capital Hattusa was excavated at Bogazkoy in 1906 and thousands of cuneiform tablets in the Hittite language were recovered from it. Uriah bears a Hebrew name meaning the LORD is my light and is counted among David's thirty (2 Samuel 23:39).

stories.keyTakeaway: David sees Bathsheba bathing, sleeps with her, and when she becomes pregnant he tries to conceal it by recalling her husband Uriah from battle; when Uriah refuses to go home, David arranges for him to be killed in combat and then takes Bathsheba as his wife.

stories.title: 🔥 2 Samuel 12
summaryBullets: Then the LORD sent Nathan to David, and when he arrived, he said, “There were two men in a certain city, one rich and the other poor. (12:1).
The rich man had a great number of sheep and cattle, (12:2).

but the poor man had nothing except one small ewe lamb that he had bought. He raised it, and it grew up with him and his children. It shared his food and drank from his cup; it slept in his arms and was like a daughter to him. (12:3).

Now a traveler came to the rich man, who refrained from taking one of his own sheep or cattle to prepare for the traveler who had come to him. Instead, he took the poor man’s lamb and prepared it for his guest.” (12:4).
David burned with anger against the man and said to Nathan: “As surely as the LORD lives, the man who did this deserves to die! (12:5).
Because he has done this thing and has shown no pity, he must pay for the lamb four times over.” (12:6).
Then Nathan said to David, “You are that man! This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you from the hand of Saul. (12:7).
I gave your master’s house to you and your master’s wives into your arms. I gave you the house of Israel and Judah, and if that was not enough, I would have given you even more. (12:8).

Why then have you despised the command of the LORD by doing evil in His sight? You put Uriah the Hittite to the sword and took his wife as your own. You have slain him with the sword of the Ammonites. (12:9).
Now, therefore, the sword will never depart from your house, because you have despised Me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your own.’ (12:10).

This is what the LORD says: ‘I will raise up adversity against you from your own house. Before your very eyes I will take your wives and give them to another, and he will lie with them in broad daylight. (12:11).
You have acted in secret, but I will do this thing in broad daylight before all Israel.’” (12:12).
Then David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” “The LORD has taken away your sin,” Nathan replied. “You will not die. (12:13).
Nevertheless, because by this deed you have shown utter contempt for the word of the LORD, the son born to you will surely die.” (12:14).
After Nathan had gone home, the LORD struck the child that Uriah’s wife had borne to David, and he became ill. (12:15).
David pleaded with God for the boy. He fasted and went into his house and spent the night lying in sackcloth on the ground. (12:16).
The elders of his household stood beside him to help him up from the ground, but he was unwilling and would not eat anything with them. (12:17).

On the seventh day the child died. But David’s servants were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, “Look, while the child was alive, we spoke to him, and he would not listen to us. So how can we tell him the child is dead? He may even harm himself.” (12:18).
When David saw that his servants were whispering to one another, he perceived that the child was dead. So he asked his servants, “Is the child dead?” “He is dead,” they replied. (12:19).

Then David got up from the ground, washed and anointed himself, changed his clothes, and went into the house of the LORD and worshiped. Then he went to his own house, and at his request they set food before him, and he ate. (12:20).
“What is this you have done?” his servants asked. “While the child was alive, you fasted and wept, but when he died, you got up and ate.” (12:21).
David answered, “While the child was alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, ‘Who knows? The LORD may be gracious to me and let him live.’ (12:22).
But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.” (12:23).
Then David comforted his wife Bathsheba, and he went to her and lay with her. So she gave birth to a son, and they named him Solomon. Now the LORD loved the child (12:24).
and sent word through Nathan the prophet to name him Jedidiah because the LORD loved him. (12:25).
Meanwhile, Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the royal fortress. (12:26).
Then Joab sent messengers to David to say, “I have fought against Rabbah and have captured the water supply of the city. (12:27).
Now, therefore, assemble the rest of the troops, lay siege to the city, and capture it. Otherwise I will capture the city, and it will be named after me.” (12:28).
So David assembled all the troops and went to Rabbah; and he fought against it and captured it. (12:29).

Then he took the crown from the head of their king. It weighed a talent of gold and was set with precious stones, and it was placed on David’s head. And David took a great amount of plunder from the city. (12:30).

David brought out the people who were there and put them to work with saws, iron picks, and axes, and he made them work at the brick kilns. He did the same to all the Ammonite cities. Then David and all his troops returned to Jerusalem. (12:31).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 11:1-27: The events Nathan is answering, from the roof to the letter carried by Uriah himself.
Exodus 22:1: A man who steals a sheep and kills it repays four sheep, the fourfold sentence David passes on himself.
Psalm 51:1-19: David's confession, headed as from when Nathan the prophet came to him after Bathsheba.
2 Samuel 16:20-22: Absalom goes in to his father's concubines on the roof in the sight of all Israel.
1 Chronicles 20:1-3: The parallel account of the fall of Rabbah, the crown of a talent of gold, and the forced labour.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָטָא (chata), to miss - Greek (LXX): ἁμαρτία (hamartia)
translationNotes.note: Chata is the plain verb for missing a target; Judges 20:16 uses it of slingers who do not miss a hair. David's answer in verse 13 is three words in Hebrew, chatati la-YHWH, I have sinned against the LORD, and Nathan's reply comes back in the same breath. The heading attached to Psalm 51 names this occasion, and that psalm reaches for three different words in its first two verses: transgression, iniquity, and this one.

The Hebrew word behind repent is not about feeling; it is the ordinary verb for turning round and going back, used of a traveller or an army. What the prophets ask for is a change of direction that can be seen from outside. This chapter shows the difference between remorse and repentance in one man across a fortnight: verses 16 to 20 have David fasting and lying on the ground for seven days over the child, then washing, anointing himself and going in to worship the moment the child dies.

David's own sentence in verse 6, that the man must repay the lamb four times over, is a quotation of the statute.
