Exodus 22:1 requires four sheep for one sheep stolen and slaughtered, and five oxen for an ox. He is not inventing a penalty in anger; he is applying the law he knows, correctly, to a case he has not yet realised is his own. Nathan then answers in verse 7 with four words in Hebrew, you are the man.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רַבָּה (Rabbah) - עִיר הַמָּיִם (ir ha-mayim), the city of waters
translationNotes.note: Rabbah was the Ammonite capital, on the upper reaches of the Jabbok where modern Amman stands, and the siege that opens at 11:1 is still running here. Verse 27 explains how a siege was actually won: Joab reports that he has taken the water supply, the lower town over the springs, which means the citadel above cannot hold out and is now only waiting. He then sends for the king so the credit for the capture goes where it belongs.

The largest unit of weight and money in the ancient world. A talent of silver weighed about 75 lbs (34 kg) and equaled roughly 6,000 denarii; about 20 years of a laborer's wages. A talent of gold was worth far more. When Jesus tells the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), each talent represents a staggering trust.

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

translationNotes.term: Lay on the ground and fasted
translationNotes.note: Verses 16 to 20 set out the standard signs of mourning and pleading: fasting, sleeping on the bare ground, refusing to wash, anoint, or change clothes. Anointing with olive oil was daily grooming in a hot, dry country, so going unanointed was visible to everyone. David's servants are frightened in verse 18 because he does all of it before the death and none of it afterward.

stories.keyTakeaway: Nathan confronts David with a parable about a rich man stealing a poor man's lamb, then reveals that David himself is that man for taking Uriah's wife and arranging Uriah's death; David confesses his sin, the child born to him and Bathsheba dies despite his fasting and prayer, and later David and Bathsheba conceive Solomon, whom the LORD loves. Joab captures Rabbah of the Ammonites, and David takes the city, plunders it, and enslaves its people.

stories.title: 💔 2 Samuel 13
summaryBullets: After some time, David’s son Amnon fell in love with Tamar, the beautiful sister of David’s son Absalom. (13:1).
Amnon was sick with frustration over his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed implausible for him to do anything to her. (13:2).
Now Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, the son of David’s brother Shimeah. Jonadab was a very shrewd man, (13:3).
and he asked Amnon, “Why are you, the son of the king, so depressed morning after morning? Won’t you tell me?” Amnon replied, “I am in love with Tamar, my brother Absalom’s sister.” (13:4).

Jonadab told him, “Lie down on your bed and pretend you are ill. When your father comes to see you, say to him, ‘Please let my sister Tamar come and give me something to eat. Let her prepare it in my sight so I may watch her and eat it from her hand.’” (13:5).
So Amnon lay down and feigned illness. When the king came to see him, Amnon said, “Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in my sight, so that I may eat from her hand.” (13:6).
Then David sent word to Tamar at the palace: “Please go to the house of Amnon your brother and prepare a meal for him.” (13:7).
So Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, who was lying down. She took some dough, kneaded it, made cakes in his sight, and baked them. (13:8).
Then she brought the pan and set it down before him, but he refused to eat. “Send everyone away!” said Amnon. And everyone went out. (13:9).
Then Amnon said to Tamar, “Bring the food into the bedroom, so that I may eat it from your hand.” Tamar took the cakes she had made and went to her brother Amnon’s bedroom. (13:10).
And when she had brought them to him to eat, he took hold of her and said, “Come lie with me, my sister!” (13:11).
“No, my brother!” she cried. “Do not violate me, for such a thing should never be done in Israel. Do not do this disgraceful thing! (13:12).
Where could I ever take my shame? And you would be like one of the fools in Israel! Please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you.” (13:13).
But Amnon refused to listen to her, and being stronger, he violated her and lay with her. (13:14).
Then Amnon hated Tamar with such intensity that his hatred was greater than the love he previously had. “Get up!” he said to her. “Be gone!” (13:15).
“No,” she replied, “sending me away is worse than this great wrong you have already done to me!” But he refused to listen to her. (13:16).
Instead, he called to his attendant and said, “Throw this woman out and bolt the door behind her!” (13:17).
So Amnon’s attendant threw her out and bolted the door behind her. Now Tamar was wearing a robe of many colors, because this is what the king’s virgin daughters wore. (13:18).
And Tamar put ashes on her head and tore her robe. And putting her hand on her head, she went away crying aloud. (13:19).

Her brother Absalom said to her, “Has your brother Amnon been with you? Be quiet for now, my sister. He is your brother. Do not take this thing to heart.” So Tamar lived as a desolate woman in the house of her brother Absalom. (13:20).
When King David heard all this, he was furious. (13:21).
And Absalom never said a word to Amnon, either good or bad, because he hated Amnon for violating his sister Tamar. (13:22).
Two years later, when Absalom’s sheepshearers were at Baal-hazor near Ephraim, he invited all the sons of the king. (13:23).
And he went to the king and said, “Your servant has just hired shearers. Will the king and his servants please come with me?” (13:24).
“No, my son,” the king replied, “we should not all go, or we would be a burden to you.” Although Absalom urged him, he was not willing to go, but gave him his blessing. (13:25).
“If not,” said Absalom, “please let my brother Amnon go with us.” “Why should he go with you?” the king asked. (13:26).
But Absalom urged him, so the king sent Amnon and the rest of his sons. (13:27).

Now Absalom had ordered his young men, “Watch Amnon until his heart is merry with wine, and when I order you to strike Amnon down, you are to kill him. Do not be afraid. Have I not commanded you? Be courageous and valiant!” (13:28).
So Absalom’s young men did to Amnon just as Absalom had ordered. Then all the other sons of the king got up, and each one fled on his mule. (13:29).
While they were on the way, a report reached David: “Absalom has struck down all the sons of the king; not one of them is left!” (13:30).
Then the king stood up, tore his clothes, and lay down on the ground. And all his servants stood by with their clothes torn. (13:31).

But Jonadab, the son of David’s brother Shimeah, spoke up: “My lord must not think they have killed all the sons of the king, for only Amnon is dead. In fact, Absalom has planned this since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar. (13:32).
So now, my lord the king, do not take to heart the report that all the sons of the king are dead. Only Amnon is dead.” (13:33).

Meanwhile, Absalom had fled. When the young man standing watch looked up, he saw many people coming down the road west of him, along the side of the hill. And the watchman went and reported to the king, “I see men coming from the direction of Horonaim, along the side of the hill.” (13:34).
So Jonadab said to the king, “Look, the sons of the king have arrived! It is just as your servant said.” (13:35).
And as he finished speaking, the sons of the king came in, wailing loudly. Then the king and all his servants also wept very bitterly. (13:36).
Now Absalom fled and went to Talmai son of Ammihud, the king of Geshur. But David mourned for his son every day. (13:37).
After Absalom had fled and gone to Geshur, he stayed there three years. (13:38).
And King David longed to go to Absalom, for he had been consoled over Amnon’s death. (13:39).
crossRefs: Leviticus 18:9,11: You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, the daughter of your father or of your mother.
Deuteronomy 22:25-29: The law for the man who forces a betrothed woman, and for the one who violates an unbetrothed virgin.
Genesis 34:1-7: Dinah is violated at Shechem, and Jacob's sons come in from the field in fury.
2 Samuel 3:2-3: Absalom is born to Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, the grandfather he flees to in verse 37.
2 Samuel 12:10-12: Nathan's word that the sword would never depart from David's house and that evil would rise out of it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָנָה (anah), to force or humiliate - נְבָלָה (nevalah), an outrage
translationNotes.note: Verses 12 and 14 use the vocabulary the law uses. Anah means to force down or violate, and it is the verb in Deuteronomy 22:29 and in Genesis 34:2 of Dinah. Tamar's own word in verse 12 is nevalah, an outrage, the term used of the crime at Gibeah (Judges 19:23-24) and of Shechem's act (Genesis 34:7); it names a deed that breaks the community's most basic order, not merely a sin against her. Verse 14 records that he would not listen and was stronger than she was, and forced her.

Verse 15 is written as a reversal in one sentence: Amnon hated her with a hatred greater than the love with which he had loved her. The same pair of words is set against each other in the law about a man with two wives, the loved and the hated (Deuteronomy 21:15-17), where hated is a legal status meaning set aside, not merely disliked. Throwing her out and bolting the door behind her, which is verses 16 to 18, is that status made public in the street.

translationNotes.term: She put ashes on her head
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵפֶר (efer), ashes - יָד עַל־רֹאשׁ (yad al rosh), hand on the head
translationNotes.note: Verse 19 is a set of recognised signs performed in the open where everyone will see them: ashes on the head, the robe torn, a hand laid on the head, and crying aloud as she goes. Hands on the head is the gesture of a captive or of shame, used at Jeremiah 2:37. Tamar has been told to keep quiet, and instead she puts on the full public display of mourning, which is the only testimony available to her.

The word verse 20 uses of Tamar living in her brother's house is the one used of a ruined city or a land emptied of people (Isaiah 54:1, Lamentations 1:16). Unmarried and unmarriageable, she has no household of her own and no children, which in that society meant no place and no future; she lives on inside Absalom's household. Two years later he names his own daughter Tamar (14:27).

Verse 18 says this is what the virgin daughters of the king wore, and it is the exact phrase used of the coat Jacob gave Joseph (Genesis 37:3). It marked a person who did not work, since long sleeves and a full-length skirt are useless for labour. Tamar tearing it in verse 19 is a public declaration that the status it announced is gone.

stories.keyTakeaway: Amnon tricks his father David into sending Tamar to his bedroom, where he rapes her; two years later, Absalom avenges his sister by having Amnon murdered at a sheepshearing feast, then flees to Geshur. David mourns for Amnon while longing to see his fugitive son Absalom.

stories.title: 💔 2 Samuel 14
summaryBullets: Now Joab son of Zeruiah perceived that the king’s heart longed for Absalom. (14:1).

So Joab sent to Tekoa to bring a wise woman from there. He told her, “Please pretend to be a mourner; put on clothes for mourning and do not anoint yourself with oil. Act like a woman who has mourned for the dead a long time. (14:2).
Then go to the king and speak these words to him.” And Joab put the words in her mouth. (14:3).
When the woman from Tekoa went to the king, she fell facedown in homage and said, “Help me, O king!” (14:4).
“What troubles you?” the king asked her. “Indeed,” she said, “I am a widow, for my husband is dead. (14:5).
And your maidservant had two sons who were fighting in the field with no one to separate them, and one struck the other and killed him. (14:6).

Now the whole clan has risen up against your maidservant and said, ‘Hand over the one who struck down his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of the brother whom he killed. Then we will cut off the heir as well!’ So they would extinguish my one remaining ember by not preserving my husband’s name or posterity on the earth.” (14:7).
“Go home,” the king said to the woman, “and I will give orders on your behalf.” (14:8).
But the woman of Tekoa said to the king, “My lord the king, may any blame be on me and on my father’s house, and may the king and his throne be guiltless.” (14:9).
“If anyone speaks to you,” said the king, “bring him to me, and he will not trouble you again!” (14:10).

“Please,” she replied, “may the king invoke the LORD your God to prevent the avenger of blood from increasing the devastation, so that my son may not be destroyed!” “As surely as the LORD lives,” he vowed, “not a hair of your son’s head will fall to the ground.” (14:11).
Then the woman said, “Please, may your servant speak a word to my lord the king?” “Speak,” he replied. (14:12).
The woman asked, “Why have you devised a thing like this against the people of God? When the king says this, does he not convict himself, since he has not brought back his own banished son? (14:13).

For we will surely die and be like water poured out on the ground, which cannot be recovered. Yet God does not take away a life, but He devises ways that the banished one may not be cast out from Him. (14:14).

Now therefore, I have come to present this matter to my lord the king because the people have made me afraid. Your servant thought, ‘I will speak to the king. Perhaps he will grant the request of his maidservant. (14:15).
For the king will hear and deliver his maidservant from the hand of the man who would cut off both me and my son from God’s inheritance.’ (14:16).

And now your servant says, ‘May the word of my lord the king bring me rest, for my lord the king is able to discern good and evil, just like the angel of God. May the LORD your God be with you.’” (14:17).
Then the king said to the woman, “I am going to ask you something; do not conceal it from me!” “Let my lord the king speak,” she replied. (14:18).

So the king asked, “Is the hand of Joab behind all this?” The woman answered, “As surely as you live, my lord the king, no one can turn to the right or to the left from anything that my lord the king says. Yes, your servant Joab is the one who gave me orders; he told your maidservant exactly what to say. (14:19).
Joab your servant has done this to bring about this change of affairs, but my lord has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God, to know everything that happens in the land.” (14:20).
Then the king said to Joab, “I hereby grant this request. Go, bring back the young man Absalom.” (14:21).
Joab fell facedown in homage and blessed the king. “Today,” said Joab, “your servant knows that he has found favor in your eyes, my lord the king, because the king has granted his request.” (14:22).
So Joab got up, went to Geshur, and brought Absalom to Jerusalem. (14:23).
But the king added, “He may return to his house, but he must not see my face.” So Absalom returned to his own house, but he did not see the face of the king. (14:24).
Now there was not a man in all Israel as handsome and highly praised as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the top of his head, he did not have a single flaw. (14:25).
And when he cut the hair of his head— he shaved it every year because his hair got so heavy— he would weigh it out to be two hundred shekels, according to the royal standard. (14:26).
Three sons were born to Absalom, and a daughter named Tamar, who was a beautiful woman. (14:27).
Now Absalom lived in Jerusalem two years without seeing the face of the king. (14:28).
Then he sent for Joab to send him to the king, but Joab refused to come to him. So Absalom sent a second time, but Joab still would not come. (14:29).
Then Absalom said to his servants, “Look, Joab’s field is next to mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it on fire!” And Absalom’s servants set the field on fire. (14:30).
Then Joab came to Absalom’s house and demanded, “Why did your servants set my field on fire?” (14:31).

“Look,” said Absalom, “I sent for you and said, ‘Come here. I want to send you to the king to ask: Why have I come back from Geshur? It would be better for me if I were still there.’ So now, let me see the king’s face, and if there is iniquity in me, let him kill me.” (14:32).
So Joab went and told the king, and David summoned Absalom, who came to him and bowed facedown before him. Then the king kissed Absalom. (14:33).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 12:1-7: Nathan uses a story about another man to make David pass sentence on himself.
Numbers 35:19-27: The avenger of blood may put the murderer to death, and the limits the law sets on him.
Deuteronomy 19:11-13: Deliberate murder is not covered by the cities of refuge; the elders hand the man over.
2 Samuel 18:9-15: Absalom's head catches fast in the oak and Joab drives three javelins into his heart.
Amos 1:1: Amos was among the shepherds of Tekoa, the town this woman was brought from.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִשָּׁה חֲכָמָה (ishah chakhamah), a wise woman
translationNotes.note: Tekoa is a village about ten miles south of Jerusalem on the lip of the Judean wilderness, later the home of the prophet Amos (Amos 1:1). A wise woman was a recognised figure with standing, not simply a clever one: another negotiates the surrender of a whole city and speaks for it from the wall at 20:16-22. Joab picks one, coaches her, and sends her to argue a made-up lawsuit in front of the king, because a legal petition was the one way an ordinary person could get the king's ear.

translationNotes.term: The avenger of blood in her story
translationNotes.note: Her invented case in verses 6 and 7 is built to trap. One son has killed the other in a field with no witnesses, and now the whole clan is demanding the survivor be handed over for execution, which would leave her with no heir and put the family land in other hands. That was the real procedure: the dead man's kin pursued the killer, and the clan decided. The king's ruling in verse 11, that not a hair of her son's head shall fall to the ground, is the precedent she then turns on him about Absalom.

Joab's instructions in verse 2 amount to a costume, and they list the standard signals: put on mourning clothes, do not anoint yourself with oil, and behave like a woman who has been grieving a long time. Anointing with olive oil was daily grooming in a hot dry country, so going without it was visible at a glance, and 12:20 has David resume washing, anointing and changing clothes the moment his mourning ends. She is dressed as a long-term widow so the king will hear a case about a dead son.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶבֶן הַמֶּלֶךְ (even ha-melekh), the king's weight
translationNotes.note: Verse 26 has Absalom cut his hair once a year and weigh it at two hundred shekels by the royal standard, about five pounds. Kingdoms kept an official weight standard the way they kept a treasury, and prices and taxes were reckoned against it. The detail is recorded because of how it ends in chapter 18.

stories.keyTakeaway: Joab orchestrates a woman's appeal to David about a family feud, which mirrors David's estrangement from Absalom and persuades him to allow Absalom's return from exile; after two years in Jerusalem without seeing David's face, Absalom burns Joab's field to force a meeting with the king, and David finally embraces him.

stories.title: 💔 2 Samuel 15
summaryBullets: Some time later, Absalom provided for himself a chariot with horses and fifty men to run ahead of him. (15:1).

He would get up early and stand beside the road leading to the city gate. Whenever anyone had a grievance to bring before the king for a decision, Absalom would call out and ask, “What city are you from?” And if he replied, “Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel,” (15:2).
Absalom would say, “Look, your claims are good and right, but the king has no deputy to hear you.” (15:3).
And he would add, “If only someone would appoint me judge in the land, then everyone with a grievance or dispute could come to me, and I would give him justice.” (15:4).
Also, when anyone approached to bow down to him, Absalom would reach out his hand, take hold of him, and kiss him. (15:5).
Absalom did this to all the Israelites who came to the king for justice. In this way he stole the hearts of the men of Israel. (15:6).
After four years had passed, Absalom said to the king, “Please let me go to Hebron to fulfill a vow I have made to the LORD. (15:7).
For your servant made a vow while dwelling in Geshur of Aram, saying: ‘If indeed the LORD brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship the LORD in Hebron.’” (15:8).
“Go in peace,” said the king. So Absalom got up and went to Hebron. (15:9).
Then Absalom sent spies throughout the tribes of Israel with this message: “When you hear the sound of the horn, you are to say, ‘Absalom reigns in Hebron!’” (15:10).
Two hundred men from Jerusalem accompanied Absalom. They had been invited as guests and they went along innocently, for they knew nothing about the matter. (15:11).

While Absalom was offering the sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counselor, to come from his hometown of Giloh. So the conspiracy gained strength, and Absalom’s following kept increasing. (15:12).
Then a messenger came to David and reported, “The hearts of the men of Israel are with Absalom.” (15:13).

And David said to all the servants with him in Jerusalem, “Arise and let us flee, or we will not escape from Absalom! We must leave quickly, or he will soon overtake us, heap disaster on us, and put the city to the sword.” (15:14).
The king’s servants replied, “Whatever our lord the king decides, we are your servants.” (15:15).
Then the king set out, and his entire household followed him. But he left behind ten concubines to take care of the palace. (15:16).
So the king set out with all the people following him. He stopped at the last house, (15:17).
and all his servants marched past him — all the Cherethites and Pelethites, and six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath. (15:18).
Then the king said to Ittai the Gittite, “Why should you also go with us? Go back and stay with the new king, since you are both a foreigner and an exile from your homeland. (15:19).

In fact, you arrived only yesterday; should I make you wander around with us today while I do not know where I am going? Go back and take your brothers with you. May the LORD show you loving devotion and faithfulness.” (15:20).
But Ittai answered the king, “As surely as the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king may be, whether it means life or death, there will your servant be!” (15:21).
“March on then,” said David to Ittai. So Ittai the Gittite marched past with all his men and all the little ones who were with him. (15:22).
Everyone in the countryside was weeping loudly as all the people passed by. And as the king crossed the Kidron Valley, all the people also passed toward the way of the wilderness. (15:23).

Zadok was also there, and all the Levites with him were carrying the ark of the covenant of God. And they set down the ark of God, and Abiathar offered sacrifices until all the people had passed out of the city. (15:24).
Then the king said to Zadok, “Return the ark of God to the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, He will bring me back and let me see both it and His dwelling place again. (15:25).
But if He should say, ‘I do not delight in you,’ then here I am; let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him.” (15:26).
The king also said to Zadok the priest, “Are you not a seer? Return to the city in peace— you with your son Ahimaaz, and Abiathar with his son Jonathan. (15:27).
See, I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me.” (15:28).
So Zadok and Abiathar returned the ark of God to Jerusalem and stayed there. (15:29).

But David continued up the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went up. His head was covered, and he was walking barefoot. And all the people with him covered their heads and went up, weeping as they went. (15:30).
Now someone told David: “Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.” So David pleaded, “O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness!” (15:31).
When David came to the summit, where he used to worship God, Hushai the Archite was there to meet him with his robe torn and dust on his head. (15:32).
David said to him, “If you go on with me, you will be a burden to me. (15:33).

But you can thwart the counsel of Ahithophel for me if you return to the city and say to Absalom: ‘I will be your servant, my king; in the past I was your father’s servant, but now I will be your servant.’ (15:34).
Will not Zadok and Abiathar the priests be there with you? Report to them everything you hear from the king’s palace. (15:35).
Indeed, their two sons, Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar, are there with them. Send them to me with everything you hear.” (15:36).
So David’s friend Hushai arrived in Jerusalem just as Absalom was entering the city. (15:37).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 16:18-20: Judges and officers in all your towns are to judge with righteous judgment and take no bribe.
2 Samuel 16:20-17:23: Ahithophel's counsel to Absalom, and how Hushai turns it aside.
2 Samuel 19:9-10: The tribes argue among themselves that Absalom, whom they anointed over them, has died in battle.
Psalm 3:1-8: A psalm of David headed as from when he fled from Absalom his son.
John 18:1: Jesus goes out with His disciples across the brook Kidron, the crossing David makes in verse 23.

translationNotes.note: Verse 1 is a claim to the throne made without a word being said. A chariot and horses and a body of men running ahead to clear the road were royal display, and Samuel had listed exactly this among the things a king would take: he will take your sons and appoint them to his chariots and to run before his chariots (1 Samuel 8:11). Adonijah stages the identical scene when he makes his own bid years later (1 Kings 1:5). Everyone who saw it knew what it meant.

Ahithophel held a formal post at court, and 16:23 measures his weight: his counsel was treated as though a man had enquired of the word of God. He comes from Giloh in the hills of Judah. The book also supplies, without ever joining them up, the reason he might change sides: 23:34 lists Eliam son of Ahithophel among David's thirty, and 11:3 names Bathsheba as the daughter of Eliam. Losing him is the one thing David prays about as he leaves the city (verse 31).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גִּתִּי (Gitti), a man of Gath
translationNotes.note: Verses 18 to 22 have six hundred men from Gath march past the king, led by a Philistine who arrived only yesterday. Six hundred is the exact size of the band David himself had commanded as a Philistine vassal at Ziklag (1 Samuel 27:2), and it is the standing size of such a body in this period. David tells him to go back because he is a foreigner and an exile with no stake in this; Ittai swears by the LORD and by the king and stays, and by 18:2 he commands a third of the army.

This is the second time David leaves everything and runs, and the book sets the two side by side. He fled Saul as a young man and lived in the wilderness with a band of outlaws; here he walks out of his own capital at the head of his household, up the Mount of Olives, barefoot with his head covered and weeping (verse 30). Head covered, feet bare and open weeping are the recognised public signs of mourning, worn on the road so that everyone who saw the column knew what it was.

translationNotes.term: Beside the way of the gate
translationNotes.note: A city gate was a deep chambered structure with benches, and it was where the town's public life happened: elders heard cases there, contracts were witnessed there, and anyone with a lawsuit went there first (Ruth 4:1-11, Proverbs 31:23). Absalom stands beside the road into it and intercepts people before they reach the court. He is not chatting; he is taking over the courthouse door.

stories.keyTakeaway: Absalom gains popular support by posturing as a judge and then requests permission to go to Hebron, where he launches a rebellion and claims kingship; David learns of the conspiracy and flees Jerusalem with his officials, sending back Zadok, Abiathar, and Hushai to act as informants.

headings.text: David Weeps at the Mount of Olives

stories.title: ⚔️ 2 Samuel 16
summaryBullets: When David had gone a little beyond the summit, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth was there to meet him. He had a pair of saddled donkeys loaded with two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a skin of wine. (16:1).

“Why do you have these?” asked the king. Ziba replied, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride, the bread and summer fruit are for the young men to eat, and the wine is to refresh those who become exhausted in the wilderness.” (16:2).

“Where is your master’s grandson?” asked the king. And Ziba answered, “Indeed, he is staying in Jerusalem, for he has said, ‘Today, the house of Israel will restore to me the kingdom of my grandfather.’” (16:3).
So the king said to Ziba, “All that belongs to Mephibosheth is now yours!” “I humbly bow before you,” said Ziba. “May I find favor in your eyes, my lord the king!” (16:4).
As King David approached Bahurim, a man from the family of the house of Saul was just coming out. His name was Shimei son of Gera, and as he approached, he kept yelling out curses. (16:5).
He threw stones at David and at all the servants of the king, though the troops and all the mighty men were on David’s right and left. (16:6).
And as he yelled curses, Shimei said, “Get out, get out, you worthless man of bloodshed! (16:7).

The LORD has paid you back for all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has delivered the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. See, you have come to ruin because you are a man of bloodshed!” (16:8).
Then Abishai son of Zeruiah said to the king, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and cut off his head!” (16:9).
But the king replied, “What have I to do with you, O sons of Zeruiah? If he curses me because the LORD told him, ‘Curse David,’ who can ask, ‘Why did you do this?’” (16:10).

Then David said to Abishai and to all his servants, “Behold, my own son, my own flesh and blood, seeks my life. How much more, then, this Benjamite! Leave him alone and let him curse me, for the LORD has told him so. (16:11).
Perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and repay me with good for the cursing I receive today.” (16:12).
So David and his men proceeded along the road as Shimei went along the ridge of the hill opposite him. As Shimei went, he yelled curses, threw stones, and flung dust at David. (16:13).
Finally, the king and all the people with him arrived, exhausted. And there he refreshed himself. (16:14).
Then Absalom and all the men of Israel came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him. (16:15).
And David’s friend Hushai the Archite went to Absalom and said to him, “Long live the king! Long live the king!” (16:16).
“Is this the loyalty you show your friend?” Absalom replied. “Why did you not go with your friend?” (16:17).
“Not at all,” Hushai answered. “For the one chosen by the LORD, by this people, and by all the men of Israel — his I will be, and with him I will remain. (16:18).
Furthermore, whom should I serve if not his son? As I served in your father’s presence, so also I will serve in yours.” (16:19).
Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Give me counsel. What should we do?” (16:20).

Ahithophel replied, “Sleep with your father’s concubines, whom he has left to take care of the palace. When all Israel hears that you have become a stench to your father, then the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened.” (16:21).
So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof, and he slept with his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel. (16:22).
Now in those days the advice of Ahithophel was like the consultation of the word of God. Such was the regard that both David and Absalom had for Ahithophel’s advice. (16:23).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 9:1-13: David restores all of Saul's land to Mephibosheth and gives him a place at the king's table.
2 Samuel 19:24-30: Mephibosheth says Ziba deceived him, and David splits the land between the two of them.
Exodus 22:28: You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people.
2 Samuel 12:11-12: The word that God would take David's wives and give them to his neighbour in the sight of the sun.
1 Kings 2:8-9,36-46: David's charge to Solomon about Shimei, and how Solomon finally settles the account.

translationNotes.note: Verses 1 to 4 are a property transfer done on one man's word with the other party absent. Ziba meets the fleeing king with a loaded donkey train, reports that his master has stayed in Jerusalem hoping to get Saul's kingdom back, and walks away with the whole estate. Mephibosheth gives the opposite account at 19:24-30, and David, unable to test either story, splits the land between them. The chapter shows what happens to justice when the king is on the road.

translationNotes.term: Shimei of the house of Saul
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אִישׁ הַדָּמִים (ish ha-damim), man of blood
translationNotes.note: Verse 5 identifies Shimei as a Benjaminite of Saul's own family, which is the whole point of what he shouts. His charge in verses 7 and 8 is that David is a man of blood who took the throne of Saul's house and is now being repaid; it is the northern grievance, spoken out loud on the road by a man who thinks the reckoning has finally come. Throwing stones and flinging dust are formal acts of contempt, not a loss of temper.

Hushai's cry in verse 16 is the fixed acclamation shouted at a coronation, and it is what makes it usable as a deception; the words commit him to nothing, because he does not say which king. The same shout goes up for Saul at 1 Samuel 10:24, for Solomon at 1 Kings 1:34 and 39, and for the boy Joash when the guard crowns him in the temple at 2 Kings 11:12.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל (le-ene kol Yisrael), in the sight of all Israel
translationNotes.note: Ahithophel's advice in verse 21 is a political calculation, and verse 22 shows how it was carried out: a tent pitched on the palace roof, the highest and most visible point in the city. Taking a king's women was the standard way of claiming his throne, and it only works as a claim if it is seen, which is why it is done on the roof and not indoors. Nathan had told David at 12:11-12 that this would be done to him in broad daylight.

A pilegesh was a secondary wife: a genuine and recognised marriage, but without the standing, the settlement or the family backing of a full wife, and her sons ranked below the wife's. Because the women of a royal household went with the throne, they became an instrument of politics: Abner is accused of taking Saul's concubine (3:7), Absalom takes his father's here, and Solomon reads Adonijah's request for Abishag as a bid for the crown and has him killed for it (1 Kings 2:22). The ten women in this chapter are shut up under guard for the rest of their lives (20:3).

stories.keyTakeaway: Ziba presents David supplies and claims Mephibosheth stayed in Jerusalem hoping to reclaim Saul's throne, so David gives Ziba all of Mephibosheth's property; meanwhile Shimei curses David and throws stones at him as he flees, and David refuses to retaliate. Absalom enters Jerusalem with his army and advisors; Hushai gains his confidence by pledging allegiance, and Ahithophel advises Absalom to sleep with David's concubines publicly to turn Israel fully against his father.

headings.text: The Counsel of Ahithophel and Hushai

stories.title: ⚔️ 2 Samuel 17
summaryBullets: Furthermore, Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Let me choose twelve thousand men and set out tonight in pursuit of David. (17:1).
I will attack him while he is weak and weary; I will throw him into a panic, and all the people with him will flee; I will strike down only the king (17:2).
and bring all the people back to you as a bride returning to her husband. You seek the life of only one man; then all the people will be at peace.” (17:3).
This proposal seemed good to Absalom and all the elders of Israel. (17:4).
Then Absalom said, “Summon Hushai the Archite as well, and let us hear what he too has to say.” (17:5).
So Hushai came to Absalom, who told him, “Ahithophel has spoken this proposal. Should we carry it out? If not, what do you say?” (17:6).
Hushai replied, “This time the advice of Ahithophel is not sound.” (17:7).

He continued, “You know your father and his men. They are mighty men, and as fierce as a wild bear robbed of her cubs. Moreover, your father is a man of war who will not spend the night with the troops. (17:8).
Surely by now he is hiding in a cave or some other location. If some of your troops fall first, whoever hears of it will say, ‘There has been a slaughter among the troops who follow Absalom.’ (17:9).
Then even the most valiant soldier with the heart of a lion will melt with fear, because all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man who has valiant men with him. (17:10).
Instead, I advise that all Israel from Dan to Beersheba— a multitude like the sand on the seashore— be gathered to you, and that you yourself lead them into battle. (17:11).
Then we will attack David wherever we find him, and we will descend on him like dew on the ground. And of all the men with him, not even one will remain. (17:12).
If he retreats to a city, all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we will drag it down to the valley until not even a pebble can be found there.” (17:13).

Then Absalom and all the men of Israel said, “The advice of Hushai the Archite is better than that of Ahithophel.” For the LORD had purposed to thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel in order to bring disaster on Absalom. (17:14).
So Hushai told Zadok and Abiathar, the priests, “This is what Ahithophel has advised Absalom and the elders of Israel, and this is what I have advised. (17:15).
Now send quickly and tell David, ‘Do not spend the night at the fords of the wilderness, but be sure to cross over. Otherwise the king and all the people with him will be swallowed up.’” (17:16).

Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying at En-rogel, where a servant girl would come and pass along information to them. They in turn would go and inform King David, for they dared not be seen entering the city. (17:17).
But a young man did see them and told Absalom. So the two left quickly and came to the house of a man in Bahurim. He had a well in his courtyard, and they climbed down into it. (17:18).
Then the man’s wife took a covering, spread it over the mouth of the well, and scattered grain over it so nobody would know a thing. (17:19).

When Absalom’s servants came to the woman at the house, they asked, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?” “They have crossed over the brook,” she replied. The men searched but did not find them, so they returned to Jerusalem. (17:20).

After the men had gone, Ahimaaz and Jonathan climbed up out of the well and went to inform King David, saying, “Get up and cross over the river at once, for Ahithophel has given this advice against you.” (17:21).
So David and all the people with him got up and crossed the Jordan. By daybreak, there was no one left who had not crossed the Jordan. (17:22).

When Ahithophel saw that his advice had not been followed, he saddled his donkey and set out for his house in his hometown. He put his affairs in order and hanged himself. So he died and was buried in his father’s tomb. (17:23).
Then David went to Mahanaim, and Absalom crossed the Jordan with all the men of Israel. (17:24).

Absalom had appointed Amasa over the army in place of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra, the Ishmaelite who had married Abigail, the daughter of Nahash and sister of Zeruiah the mother of Joab. (17:25).
So the Israelites and Absalom camped in the land of Gilead. (17:26).
When David came to Mahanaim, he was met by Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim. (17:27).
They brought beds, basins, and earthen vessels, as well as wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans, lentils, (17:28).
honey, curds, sheep, and cheese from the herd for David and his people to eat. For they said, “The people have become hungry, exhausted, and thirsty in the wilderness.” (17:29).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 15:31-37: David prays that Ahithophel's counsel be turned to foolishness and sends Hushai back to Jerusalem.
2 Samuel 16:23: The counsel Ahithophel gave in those days was as if a man consulted the word of God.
Joshua 2:1-7: Rahab hides the two spies under the flax on her roof and sends the pursuers off the wrong way.
Psalm 41:9: Even my close friend, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me.
Matthew 27:3-5: Judas throws the silver into the temple, goes out, and hangs himself.

translationNotes.note: A spring just south of Jerusalem, below the point where the Kidron and Hinnom valleys meet, outside the city wall. It marked the boundary between Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:7; 18:16), so it was a place a man could wait without entering the city, which is exactly why the two messengers are stationed there. Adonijah later held his coronation feast at the stone of Zoheleth beside the same spring (1 Kings 1:9).

Houses had a rock-cut cistern in the courtyard, plastered inside and fed by runoff from the roof, with a narrow mouth closed by a stone slab. Spreading grain out on the cover to dry was ordinary household work, so nothing looked wrong. Bahurim is a Benjaminite village on the ridge road running down from the Mount of Olives toward the Jordan, the same place where Shimei had thrown stones at David two chapters earlier (2 Samuel 16:5).

translationNotes.term: He put his affairs in order and hanged himself
translationNotes.note: Suicide is recorded only a handful of times in Scripture: Saul and his armour-bearer on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:4-5), Ahithophel here, Zimri burning the palace over himself (1 Kings 16:18), and Judas (Matthew 27:5). The detail that he was buried in his father's tomb matters: family tombs were rock-cut chambers with benches, where a body was laid out and the bones later gathered into a pit or a box, which is the practice behind the phrase gathered to his fathers.

A walled town east of the Jordan in Gilead. The name means two camps, and Genesis 32:1-2 records Jacob giving it that name when the angels of God met him on his way back to Canaan. It was assigned to the Levites (Joshua 21:38) and had already served as Ish-bosheth's capital (2 Samuel 2:8). David makes it his base because it is across the river, defensible, and among people who owe him nothing to Absalom.

translationNotes.term: Roasted grain, beans, lentils, curds, and cheese
translationNotes.note: This is a field ration list, and every item is what people actually carried. Qali is parched grain, new heads roasted over a fire and eaten as they are, the standard travelling food (Ruth 2:14; 1 Samuel 17:17; 25:18). Chemah is curdled milk, closer to soured cream or butter than to anything sweet. Beds and basins in verse 28 mean the district was supplying a whole camp, not sending a courtesy gift.

stories.keyTakeaway: Ahithophel advises Absalom to pursue David immediately, but Hushai counters with a plan to gather all Israel first; Absalom accepts Hushai's advice, allowing David to escape across the Jordan while Ahithophel hangs himself. David reaches Mahanaim, where local leaders provide him food and supplies.

stories.title: ⚔️ 2 Samuel 18
summaryBullets: Then David reviewed his troops and appointed over them commanders of thousands and of hundreds. (18:1).

He sent out the troops, a third under Joab, a third under Joab’s brother Abishai son of Zeruiah, and a third under Ittai the Gittite. And the king said to the troops, “I will surely march out with you as well.” (18:2).

But the people pleaded, “You must not go out! For if we have to flee, they will not care about us. Even if half of us die, they will not care. But you are worth ten thousand of us. It is better now if you support us from the city.” (18:3).
“I will do whatever seems best to you,” the king replied. So he stood beside the gate, while all the troops marched out by hundreds and by thousands. (18:4).
Now the king had commanded Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, “Treat the young man Absalom gently for my sake.” And all the people heard the king’s orders to each of the commanders regarding Absalom. (18:5).
So David’s army marched into the field to engage Israel, and the battle took place in the forest of Ephraim. (18:6).
There the people of Israel were defeated by David’s servants, and the slaughter was great that day— twenty thousand men. (18:7).
The battle spread over the whole countryside, and that day the forest devoured more people than the sword. (18:8).

Now Absalom was riding on his mule when he met the servants of David, and as the mule went under the thick branches of a large oak, Absalom’s head was caught fast in the tree. The mule under him kept going, so that he was suspended in midair. (18:9).
When one of the men saw this, he told Joab, “I just saw Absalom hanging in an oak tree!” (18:10).
“You just saw him!” Joab exclaimed. “Why did you not strike him to the ground right there? I would have given you ten shekels of silver and a warrior’s belt!” (18:11).

The man replied, “Even if a thousand shekels of silver were weighed out into my hands, I would not raise my hand against the son of the king. For we heard the king command you and Abishai and Ittai, ‘Protect the young man Absalom for my sake.’ (18:12).
If I had jeopardized my own life— and nothing is hidden from the king— you would have abandoned me.” (18:13).
But Joab declared, “I am not going to wait like this with you!” And he took three spears in his hand and thrust them through the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the oak tree. (18:14).
And ten young men who carried Joab’s armor surrounded Absalom, struck him, and killed him. (18:15).
Then Joab blew the ram’s horn, and the troops broke off their pursuit of Israel because Joab had restrained them. (18:16).
They took Absalom, cast him into a large pit in the forest, and piled a huge mound of stones over him. Meanwhile, all the Israelites fled, each to his home. (18:17).

During his lifetime, Absalom had set up for himself a pillar in the King’s Valley, for he had said, “I have no son to preserve the memory of my name.” So he gave the pillar his name, and to this day it is called Absalom’s Monument. (18:18).
Then Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, “Please let me run and tell the king the good news that the LORD has avenged him of his enemies.” (18:19).
But Joab replied, “You are not the man to take good news today. You may do it another day, but you must not do so today, because the king’s son is dead.” (18:20).
So Joab said to a Cushite, “Go, tell the king what you have seen.” The Cushite bowed to Joab and took off running. (18:21).

Ahimaaz son of Zadok, however, persisted and said to Joab, “No matter what, please let me also run behind the Cushite!” “My son,” Joab replied, “why do you want to run, since you will not receive a reward?” (18:22).
“No matter what, I want to run!” he replied. “Then run!” Joab told him. So Ahimaaz ran by way of the plain and outran the Cushite. (18:23).
Now David was sitting between the two gates when the watchman went up to the roof of the gateway by the wall, looked out, and saw a man running alone. (18:24).
So he called out and told the king. “If he is alone,” the king replied, “he bears good news.” As the first runner drew near, (18:25).
the watchman saw another man running, and he called out to the gatekeeper, “Look! Another man is running alone!” “This one also brings good news,” said the king. (18:26).
The watchman said, “The first man appears to me to be running like Ahimaaz son of Zadok.” “This is a good man,” said the king. “He comes with good news.” (18:27).

Then Ahimaaz called out to the king, “All is well!” And he bowed facedown before the king. He continued, “Blessed be the LORD your God! He has delivered up the men who raised their hands against my lord the king.” (18:28).
The king asked, “Is the young man Absalom all right?” And Ahimaaz replied, “When Joab sent the king’s servant and your servant, I saw a great tumult, but I do not know what it was.” (18:29).
“Move aside,” said the king, “and stand here.” So he stepped aside. (18:30).
Just then the Cushite came and said, “May my lord the king hear the good news: Today the LORD has avenged you of all who rose up against you!” (18:31).

The king asked the Cushite, “Is the young man Absalom all right?” And the Cushite replied, “May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you to harm you be like that young man.” (18:32).

The king was shaken and went up to the chamber over the gate and wept. And as he walked, he cried out, “O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!” (18:33).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 14:25-26: Absalom's yearly haircut, weighed at two hundred shekels by the king's weight.
Deuteronomy 21:18-21: The law for a stubborn and rebellious son who will not listen to his father or his mother.
2 Samuel 12:10-12: The word that the sword would never depart from David's house.
2 Samuel 19:1-8: Joab confronts David for shaming the men who saved his life by mourning the man who hunted him.
2 Samuel 14:27: Absalom is recorded as having three sons and a daughter, though verse 18 says he had no son to keep his name alive.

translationNotes.term: The king kept out of the battle
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲשָׂרָה אֲלָפִים (asarah alafim), ten thousand
translationNotes.note: The army refuses to let David take the field in verse 3, and their reasoning is cold arithmetic: if they run, nobody cares, and if half of them die, nobody cares, but he is worth ten thousand of them. A king in the line is the one target whose loss ends a war on the spot, which is why the enemy hunts him and why his own men would rather he sat in the gate at Mahanaim with a runner posted on the wall. His absence is also why the order about Absalom is given publicly to three commanders and then ignored.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶלֶף כֶּסֶף (eleph kesef), a thousand of silver
translationNotes.note: The soldier in verse 12 turns down a hypothetical bounty of a thousand shekels, and the figure is meant to sound enormous: a shekel weighs about two-fifths of an ounce, so this is roughly twenty-seven pounds of silver, when a Levite could be hired for ten shekels a year with board and clothing (Judges 17:10). His reason is not money but the order everyone heard the king give to Joab, Abishai and Ittai in the hearing of the whole army. Joab's answer is to take three spears and do it himself.

translationNotes.term: A heap of stones over the pit
translationNotes.note: Verse 17 gives the king's son the burial of a condemned criminal: thrown into a large pit in the forest with a great mound of stones piled on top. The same cairn goes over Achan in the Valley of Achor (Joshua 7:26) and over the king of Ai (Joshua 8:29). It is a public marker meant to be seen from the road, and it stands directly against verse 18, where Absalom had raised a pillar in the King's Valley in his own lifetime so that his name would be remembered.

translationNotes.term: His head caught fast in the oak
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵלָה (elah), terebinth or great tree
translationNotes.note: Verse 9 says his head caught in the tree, not his hair; the hair is the reader's addition. He is riding a mule under a low, thick-limbed terebinth in broken forest country, and he is left hanging between the tree and the sky when the animal keeps going. Verse 8 has already noted that the forest killed more men that day than the sword.

Verses 19 to 27 turn on the two routes out of the forest of Ephraim: the Cushite goes straight over the hills, and Ahimaaz takes the longer flat road through the Jordan plain and still arrives first. News travelled at the pace of a man on foot, and a watchman on the gate tower identified runners by their gait long before they arrived (verse 27). Being first with the news was itself a position at court.

stories.keyTakeaway: David organizes his forces into three divisions under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, then positions himself at the city gate while his troops march out; Absalom is caught by his hair in an oak tree during the battle, and Joab kills him with three javelins despite David's command to spare him. Runners bring word to David that the battle is won, but when he learns Absalom is dead, he grieves deeply in the gateway chamber, lamenting that he wishes he had died instead of his son.

stories.title: ⚔️ 2 Samuel 19
summaryBullets: Then it was reported to Joab, “The king is weeping and mourning over Absalom.” (19:1).
And that day’s victory was turned into mourning for all the people, because on that day they were told, “The king is grieving over his son.” (19:2).
So they returned to the city quietly that day, as people steal away in humiliation after fleeing a battle. (19:3).
But the king covered his face and cried out at the top of his voice, “O my son Absalom! O Absalom, my son, my son!” (19:4).

Then Joab went into the house and said to the king, “Today you have disgraced all your servants who have saved your life and the lives of your sons and daughters, of your wives, and of your concubines. (19:5).

You love those who hate you and hate those who love you! For you have made it clear today that the commanders and soldiers mean nothing to you. I know today that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead, it would have pleased you! (19:6).

Now therefore get up! Go out and speak comfort to your servants, for I swear by the LORD that if you do not go out, not a man will remain with you tonight. This will be worse for you than all the adversity that has befallen you from your youth until now!” (19:7).

So the king got up and sat in the gate, and all the people were told: “Behold, the king is sitting in the gate.” So they all came before the king. Meanwhile, the Israelites had fled, each man to his home. (19:8).

And all the people throughout the tribes of Israel were arguing, “The king rescued us from the hand of our enemies and delivered us from the hand of the Philistines, but now he has fled the land because of Absalom. (19:9).
But Absalom, the man we anointed over us, has died in battle. So why do you say nothing about restoring the king?” (19:10).

Then King David sent this message to Zadok and Abiathar, the priests: “Say to the elders of Judah, ‘Why should you be the last to restore the king to his palace, since the talk of all Israel has reached the king at his quarters? (19:11).
You are my brothers, my own flesh and blood. So why should you be the last to restore the king?’ (19:12).
And say to Amasa, ‘Aren’t you my flesh and blood? May God punish me, and ever so severely, if from now on you are not the commander of my army in place of Joab!’” (19:13).
So he swayed the hearts of all the men of Judah as though they were one man, and they sent word to the king: “Return, you and all your servants.” (19:14).
So the king returned, and when he arrived at the Jordan, the men of Judah came to Gilgal to meet him and escort him across the Jordan. (19:15).
Then Shimei son of Gera, a Benjamite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David, (19:16).
along with a thousand men of Benjamin, as well as Ziba the steward of the house of Saul and his fifteen sons and twenty servants. They rushed down to the Jordan before the king (19:17).
and crossed at the ford to carry over the king’s household and to do what was good in his sight. When Shimei son of Gera crossed the Jordan, he fell down before the king (19:18).
and said, “My lord, do not hold me guilty, and do not remember your servant’s wrongdoing on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. May the king not take it to heart. (19:19).
For your servant knows that I have sinned, so here I am today as the first of all the house of Joseph to come down to meet my lord the king.” (19:20).
But Abishai son of Zeruiah said, “Shouldn’t Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD’s anointed?” (19:21).

And David replied, “Sons of Zeruiah, what have I to do with you, that you should be my adversaries today? Should any man be put to death in Israel today? Am I not indeed aware that today I am king over Israel?” (19:22).
So the king said to Shimei, “You shall not die.” And the king swore an oath to him. (19:23).

Then Mephibosheth, Saul’s grandson, went down to meet the king. He had not cared for his feet or trimmed his mustache or washed his clothes from the day the king had left until the day he returned safely. (19:24).
And he came from Jerusalem to meet the king, who asked him, “Mephibosheth, why did you not go with me?” (19:25).
“My lord the king,” he replied, “because I am lame, I said, ‘I will have my donkey saddled so that I may ride on it and go with the king.’ But my servant Ziba deceived me, (19:26).
and he has slandered your servant to my lord the king. Yet my lord the king is like the angel of God, so do what is good in your eyes. (19:27).

For all the house of my grandfather deserves death from my lord the king, yet you have set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further right, then, do I have to keep appealing to the king?” (19:28).
The king replied, “Why say any more? I hereby declare that you and Ziba are to divide the land.” (19:29).
And Mephibosheth said to the king, “Instead, since my lord the king has safely come to his own house, let Ziba take it all!” (19:30).
Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim to cross the Jordan with the king and send him on his way from there. (19:31).
Barzillai was quite old, eighty years of age, and since he was a very wealthy man, he had provided for the king while he stayed in Mahanaim. (19:32).
The king said to Barzillai, “Cross over with me, and I will provide for you at my side in Jerusalem.” (19:33).
But Barzillai replied, “How many years of my life remain, that I should go up to Jerusalem with the king? (19:34).

I am now eighty years old. Can I discern what is good and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or drinks? Can I still hear the voice of singing men and women? Why should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king? (19:35).
Your servant will go with the king only a short distance past the Jordan; why should the king repay me with such a reward? (19:36).

Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the tomb of my father and mother. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him what is good in your sight.” (19:37).
The king replied, “Chimham will cross over with me, and I will do for him what is good in your sight, and I will do for you whatever you desire of me.” (19:38).
So all the people crossed the Jordan, and then the king crossed over. The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai returned home. (19:39).
Then the king crossed over to Gilgal, and Chimham crossed over with him. All the troops of Judah and half the troops of Israel escorted the king. (19:40).

Soon all the men of Israel came to the king and asked, “Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, take you away secretly and bring the king and his household across the Jordan, together with all of David’s men?” (19:41).

And all the men of Judah replied to the men of Israel, “We did this because the king is our relative. Why does this anger you? Have we ever eaten at the king’s expense or received anything for ourselves?” (19:42).

“We have ten shares in the king,” answered the men of Israel, “so we have more claim to David than you. Why then do you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of restoring our king?” But the men of Judah spoke more fiercely than the men of Israel. (19:43).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 16:5-13: Shimei curses David on the road at Bahurim, throwing stones and flinging dust at him.
2 Samuel 17:27-29: Barzillai the Gileadite brings beds, bowls, wheat, honey, curds, and sheep to David's people at Mahanaim.
1 Kings 2:7: David tells Solomon to show kindness to the sons of Barzillai and let them eat at his table.
2 Samuel 20:1-2: Sheba blows the trumpet and all Israel deserts David, the quarrel of verse 43 breaking into revolt.
Genesis 49:8-10: Judah, your brothers shall praise you, and your father's sons shall bow down before you.

translationNotes.term: The king sat in the gate
translationNotes.note: A city gate was a building, not an opening: a passage with guard chambers on both sides and stone benches along them, and it was where elders heard cases, contracts were witnessed, and the king gave judgment. A king sitting in the gate is a king back on duty and available, which is why the announcement in verse 8 brings the whole army in. Absalom had worked this same spot to steal the kingdom, standing beside the road into the gate and intercepting men coming for judgment (2 Samuel 15:2).

translationNotes.term: He had not cared for his feet or trimmed his mustache
translationNotes.note: These were the recognised public signs of mourning: unwashed body and clothes, untrimmed hair and beard, no oil. Sapham is the moustache, the hair of the upper lip, and covering or neglecting it belongs to the same set of grief and defilement signals as in Leviticus 13:45 and Ezekiel 24:17. The reverse marks the end of mourning: in 2 Samuel 12:20 David washes, anoints himself, and changes his clothes.

Mashiach means smeared with oil, and it is the standing term for the king because he was installed by having oil poured on his head (1 Samuel 10:1; 16:13). To curse in Hebrew, qillel, is not swearing; the root means to make light, and the act is calling down harm on someone while treating him as of no weight. Exodus 22:28 forbids cursing a ruler of your people.

Barzillai had fed the king's whole force at Mahanaim out of his own estate in Gilead, and what David offers back is a place at the royal table, which was a permanent maintenance. Barzillai sends Chimham in his place, apparently his son. Long afterwards, Jeremiah 41:17 records refugees stopping at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, a holding that still carried his name.

translationNotes.term: We have ten shares in the king
translationNotes.note: The northern tribes are doing arithmetic: ten tribes against Judah, so ten portions of the king against one. The same count runs through the split that follows a generation later, when Ahijah tears a new cloak into twelve pieces and gives ten of them to Jeroboam (1 Kings 11:30-31), and the north walks out with the cry, what share do we have in David (1 Kings 12:16). This quarrel at the Jordan is where that crack first shows.

stories.keyTakeaway: David grieves Absalom's death so deeply that his troops lose their will to celebrate their victory; Joab forces him to face his men and accept their loyalty. David returns to Jerusalem with Judah's support, pardons Shimei, divides Saul's land between Mephibosheth and Ziba, and accepts Barzillai's son Kimham into his service, though tension flares between the men of Judah and Israel over who brought the king home.

stories.title: ⚔️ 2 Samuel 20
summaryBullets: Now a worthless man named Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjamite, happened to be there, and he blew the ram’s horn and shouted: “We have no share in David, no inheritance in Jesse’s son. Every man to his tent, O Israel!” (20:1).
So all the men of Israel deserted David to follow Sheba son of Bichri. But the men of Judah stayed by their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem. (20:2).

When David returned to his palace in Jerusalem, he took the ten concubines he had left to take care of the palace, and he placed them in a house under guard. He provided for them, but he no longer slept with them. They were confined until the day of their death, living as widows. (20:3).
Then the king said to Amasa, “Summon the men of Judah to come to me within three days, and be here yourself.” (20:4).
So Amasa went to summon Judah, but he took longer than the time allotted him. (20:5).
And David said to Abishai, “Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord’s servants and pursue him, or he will find fortified cities and elude us.” (20:6).
So Joab’s men, along with the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty men, marched out of Jerusalem in pursuit of Sheba son of Bichri. (20:7).

And while they were at the great stone in Gibeon, Amasa joined them. Now Joab was dressed in military attire, with a dagger strapped to his belt. And as he stepped forward, he slipped the dagger from its sheath. (20:8).
“Are you well, my brother?” Joab asked Amasa. And with his right hand Joab grabbed Amasa by the beard to kiss him. (20:9).

Amasa was not on guard against the dagger in Joab’s hand, and Joab stabbed him in the stomach and spilled out his intestines on the ground. And Joab did not need to strike him again, for Amasa was dead. Then Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Sheba son of Bichri. (20:10).
One of Joab’s young men stood near Amasa and said, “Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David, let him follow Joab!” (20:11).

But Amasa wallowed in his blood in the middle of the road, and when the man saw that all the troops were stopping there, he dragged the body off the road into a field and threw a garment over it. (20:12).
As soon as Amasa’s body was removed from the road, all the men went on with Joab to pursue Sheba son of Bichri. (20:13).
Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel-beth-maacah and through the entire region of the Berites, who gathered together and followed him. (20:14).
And Joab’s troops came and besieged Sheba in Abel-beth-maacah and built a siege ramp against the outer rampart of the city. As all the troops with Joab were battering the wall to topple it, (20:15).
a wise woman called out from the city, “Listen! Listen! Please tell Joab to come here so that I may speak with him.” (20:16).
When he had come near to her, the woman asked, “Are you Joab?” “I am,” he replied. “Listen to the words of your servant,” she said. “I am listening,” he answered. (20:17).
Then the woman said, “Long ago they used to say, ‘Seek counsel at Abel,’ and that is how disputes were settled. (20:18).
I am among the peaceable and faithful in Israel, but you are trying to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why would you swallow up the LORD’s inheritance?” (20:19).
“Far be it!” Joab declared. “Far be it from me to swallow up or destroy! (20:20).

That is not the case. But a man named Sheba son of Bichri, from the hill country of Ephraim, has lifted up his hand against the king, against David. Deliver him alone, and I will depart from the city.” “Look,” the woman replied, “his head will be thrown to you over the wall.” (20:21).

Then the woman went to all the people with her wise counsel, and they cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri and threw it to Joab. So he blew the ram’s horn and his men dispersed from the city, each to his own home. And Joab returned to the king in Jerusalem. (20:22).
Now Joab was over the whole army of Israel; Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites; (20:23).
Adoram was in charge of the forced labor; Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder; (20:24).
Sheva was the scribe; Zadok and Abiathar were priests; (20:25).
and Ira the Jairite was David’s priest. (20:26).
crossRefs: 2 Samuel 3:26-30: Joab takes Abner aside at the gate and strikes him in the stomach, exactly as he does to Amasa here.
1 Kings 2:5-6: David charges Solomon over Joab, who shed the blood of war in a time of peace.
Deuteronomy 20:10-12: When you draw near a city to fight against it, first offer it terms of peace.
2 Samuel 19:11-13: David promises Amasa the command of the army in Joab's place.
1 Kings 15:20: Ben-hadad strikes Abel of Beth-maacah and all Chinneroth with the land of Naphtali.

translationNotes.term: What share have we in David
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵין־לָנוּ חֵלֶק בְּדָוִד (en lanu cheleq be-David)
translationNotes.note: Sheba blows a ram's horn and shouts a slogan in verse 1, and the slogan is the thing to notice. Word for word, it is what the ten northern tribes shout when they walk out on Rehoboam and split the kingdom for good: what share do we have in David, no inheritance in the son of Jesse, to your tents, O Israel (1 Kings 12:16). This is the first time it is heard, and the quarrel that produces it is the argument over precedence at the Jordan in the previous chapter.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַלְמְנוּת חַיּוּת (almenut chayyut), living widowhood
translationNotes.note: Verse 3 records what became of the women Absalom had taken on the palace roof. David provides for them but never goes in to them again, and they are kept in a guarded house until they die; the Hebrew phrase is widowhood while still alive. The law forbids a man to uncover his father's wife (Leviticus 18:8, Deuteronomy 22:30), so they cannot return to David, and as a former king's women they cannot be given to anyone else. The verse states the outcome without softening it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַתִּפֹּל (vattippol), and it fell out
translationNotes.note: Verses 8 to 10 describe a killing set up in advance. Joab steps forward in his military dress and his blade slips out of its sheath, so it is in his hand when he takes Amasa by the beard with his right hand to give him the customary kiss of greeting. Amasa, watching the empty right hand, is not guarding against the left. It is the second time Joab has killed a rival commander under cover of a friendly word, after Abner in the gate at Hebron (3:27).

Originally professional copyists of Scripture. By the New Testament era, scholar-teachers of the Law; often, though not exclusively, aligned with the Pharisees. They formed the educated religious class that adjudicated everyday halakhic questions.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אָבֵל בֵּית מַעֲכָה (Avel Beit Maakhah)
translationNotes.note: A fortified town in the far north near Dan, about twelve miles north of the Sea of Galilee, on the road up from Israel into Aram. The woman on the wall in verse 18 quotes a saying that people used to settle matters by asking counsel at Abel, and calls the town a mother in Israel. Her point is that a town with that standing does not get thrown down over one fugitive, and she settles it by throwing down Sheba's head instead.

stories.keyTakeaway: After Sheba son of Bichri blows the horn and draws the men of Israel away from David, the king orders pursuit before Sheba can reach fortified cities, and on the way Joab murders Amasa with a hidden dagger at Gibeon. Joab besieges Sheba in Abel-beth-maacah, where a wise woman persuades the city to throw Sheba’s head over the wall; Joab sounds the horn, his men disperse to their homes, and he returns to Jerusalem.

stories.title: ⛰️ 2 Samuel 21
summaryBullets: During the reign of David there was a famine for three successive years, and David sought the face of the LORD. And the LORD said, “It is because of the blood shed by Saul and his family, because he killed the Gibeonites.” (21:1).

At this, David summoned the Gibeonites and spoke to them. (Now the Gibeonites were not Israelites, but a remnant of the Amorites. The Israelites had taken an oath concerning them, but in his zeal for Israel and Judah, Saul had sought to kill them.) (21:2).
So David asked the Gibeonites, “What shall I do for you? How can I make amends so that you may bless the inheritance of the LORD?” (21:3).
The Gibeonites said to him, “We need no silver or gold from Saul or his house, nor should you put to death anyone in Israel for us.” “Whatever you ask, I will do for you,” he replied. (21:4).
And they answered the king, “As for the man who consumed us and plotted against us to exterminate us from existing within any border of Israel, (21:5).
let seven of his male descendants be delivered to us so that we may hang them before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the LORD.” “I will give them to you,” said the king. (21:6).
Now the king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, because of the oath before the LORD between David and Jonathan son of Saul. (21:7).

But the king took Armoni and Mephibosheth, the two sons whom Rizpah daughter of Aiah had borne to Saul, as well as the five sons whom Merab daughter of Saul had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite. (21:8).

And he delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on the hill before the LORD. So all seven of them fell together; they were put to death in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest. (21:9).

And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it out for herself on a rock. From the beginning of the harvest until the rain from heaven poured down on the bodies, she did not allow the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night. (21:10).
When David was told what Saul’s concubine Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, had done, (21:11).

he went and took the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the public square of Beth-shan where the Philistines had hung the bodies after they had struck down Saul at Gilboa. (21:12).
So David had the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan brought from there, and they also gathered the bones of those who had been hanged. (21:13).

And they buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in Zela in the land of Benjamin, in the tomb of Saul’s father Kish. After they had done everything the king had commanded, God answered their prayers for the land. (21:14).
Once again the Philistines waged war against Israel, and David and his servants went down and fought against the Philistines. But David became exhausted. (21:15).
Then Ishbi-benob, a descendant of Rapha, whose bronze spear weighed three hundred shekels and who was bearing a new sword, resolved to kill David. (21:16).

But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his aid, struck the Philistine, and killed him. Then David’s men swore to him, “You must never again go out with us to battle, so that the lamp of Israel may not be extinguished.” (21:17).
Some time later at Gob, there was another battle with the Philistines. At that time Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, a descendant of Rapha. (21:18).

Once again there was a battle with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan son of Jair the Bethlehemite killed the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver’s beam. (21:19).
And there was also a battle at Gath, where there was a man of great stature with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot— twenty-four in all. He too was descended from Rapha, (21:20).
and when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of David’s brother Shimei killed him. (21:21).
So these four descendants of Rapha in Gath fell at the hands of David and his servants. (21:22).
crossRefs: Joshua 9:3-27: The Gibeonites secure a treaty by claiming to come from a distant country, and Israel swears an oath to them.
Numbers 35:33: Blood pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for it except by the blood of the one who shed it.
Deuteronomy 21:22-23: A body hanged on a tree is not to be left overnight, for a hanged man is under God's curse.
1 Samuel 17:4-7: Goliath of Gath, six cubits and a span, with a spear shaft like a weaver's beam.
1 Chronicles 20:4-8: The parallel roll of the Philistine giants killed by David's men.

translationNotes.term: The Gibeonites and the broken oath
translationNotes.note: Verses 1 and 2 reach back nearly four centuries. The Gibeonites had obtained a treaty from Joshua by deception, and Israel swore to them by the LORD and kept it even after the fraud came out (Joshua 9:15-20). Saul broke that oath and tried to wipe them out, and the famine is laid at that. Verse 4 is the detail a reader should not skip: they refuse silver or gold, which is the ransom Numbers 35:31 forbids being taken for a life, and ask instead for men of the house that shed the blood.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כָּפַר (kaphar), to cover or wipe clean
translationNotes.note: David's question in verse 3 is how he shall kaphar, which English renders as make atonement or make amends. The verb means to cover over or wipe away so that a debt no longer stands, and it is the technical word for what the sacrifices do (Leviticus 16:30). Behind this chapter lies the rule that bloodshed pollutes the land itself and that nothing cleanses it except the blood of the man who shed it (Numbers 35:33), which is why the famine is read as a matter still outstanding on Saul's account.

Verses 15 to 22 close with four Philistine champions, each said to be descended from Rapha, the term behind the Rephaim, the tall peoples the Bible places in the land before Israel (Deuteronomy 2:10-11, 3:11). The details are physical and specific: Ishbi-benob's bronze spear weighed three hundred shekels, about seven and a half pounds, against the fifteen pounds of Goliath's iron spearhead at 1 Samuel 17:7, and one man at Gath had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot. Joshua 11:22 had already noted that the Anakim survived in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod.

A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.

Verses 9 and 10 set the exposure at the start of barley harvest, which is April, and say Rizpah kept the birds and the wild animals off the bodies until rain fell. The first rains come in October. She sat out on sackcloth beside her sons for something close to six months, in the open, and the law's requirement that a body be buried the same day (Deuteronomy 21:23) is what makes her vigil an accusation the king finally answers in verse 13.

stories.keyTakeaway: A three-year famine leads David to execute seven descendants of Saul to satisfy the Gibeonites, whom Saul had tried to destroy; after proper burial of the remains, God ends the famine and David's forces defeat several Philistine giants in subsequent battles.

stories.title: ⛰️ 2 Samuel 22
summaryBullets: And David sang this song to the LORD on the day the LORD had delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. (22:1).
He said: “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer. (22:2).
My God is my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation. My stronghold, my refuge, and my Savior, You save me from violence. (22:3).
I will call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised; so shall I be saved from my enemies. (22:4).
For the waves of death engulfed me; the torrents of chaos overwhelmed me. (22:5).
The cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me. (22:6).
