In my distress I called upon the LORD; I cried out to my God. And from His temple He heard my voice, and my cry for help reached His ears. (22:7).
Then the earth shook and quaked; the foundations of the heavens trembled; they were shaken because He burned with anger. (22:8).
Smoke rose from His nostrils, and consuming fire came from His mouth; glowing coals blazed forth. (22:9).
He parted the heavens and came down with dark clouds beneath His feet. (22:10).
He mounted a cherub and flew; He soared on the wings of the wind. (22:11).
He made darkness a canopy around Him, a gathering of water and thick clouds. (22:12).
From the brightness of His presence coals of fire blazed forth. (22:13).
The LORD thundered from heaven; the voice of the Most High resounded. (22:14).
He shot His arrows and scattered the foes; He hurled lightning and routed them. (22:15).
The channels of the sea appeared, and the foundations of the world were exposed at the rebuke of the LORD, at the blast of the breath of His nostrils. (22:16).
He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters. (22:17).
He rescued me from my powerful enemy, from foes too mighty for me. (22:18).
They confronted me in my day of calamity, but the LORD was my support. (22:19).
He brought me out into the open; He rescued me because He delighted in me. (22:20).
The LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness; He has repaid me according to the cleanness of my hands. (22:21).
For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God. (22:22).
For all His ordinances are before me; I have not disregarded His statutes. (22:23).
And I have been blameless before Him and kept myself from iniquity. (22:24).
So the LORD has repaid me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness in His sight. (22:25).
To the faithful You show Yourself faithful, to the blameless You show Yourself blameless; (22:26).
to the pure You show Yourself pure, but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd. (22:27).
You save an afflicted people, but Your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down. (22:28).
For You, O LORD, are my lamp; the LORD lights up my darkness. (22:29).
For in You I can charge an army; with my God I can scale a wall. (22:30).
As for God, His way is perfect; the word of the LORD is flawless. He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him. (22:31).
For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God? (22:32).
God is my strong fortress, and He makes my way clear. (22:33).
He makes my feet like those of a deer and stations me upon the heights. (22:34).
He trains my hands for battle; my arms can bend a bow of bronze. (22:35).
You have given me Your shield of salvation, and Your gentleness exalts me. (22:36).
You broaden the path beneath me so that my ankles do not give way. (22:37).
I pursued my enemies and destroyed them; I did not turn back until they were consumed. (22:38).
I devoured and crushed them so they could not rise; they have fallen under my feet. (22:39).
You have armed me with strength for battle; You have subdued my foes beneath me. (22:40).
You have made my enemies retreat before me; I destroyed those who hated me. (22:41).
They looked, but there was no one to save them — to the LORD, but He did not answer. (22:42).
I ground them as the dust of the earth; I crushed and trampled them like mud in the streets. (22:43).
You have delivered me from the strife of my people; You have preserved me as the head of nations; a people I had not known shall serve me. (22:44).
Foreigners cower before me; when they hear me, they obey me. (22:45).
Foreigners lose heart and come trembling from their strongholds. (22:46).
The LORD lives, and blessed be my Rock! And may God, the Rock of my salvation, be exalted— (22:47).
the God who avenges me and brings down nations beneath me, (22:48).
who frees me from my enemies. You exalt me above my foes; You rescue me from violent men. (22:49).
Therefore I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing praises to Your name. (22:50).
Great salvation He brings to His king. He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever.” (22:51).
crossRefs: Psalm 18:1-50: The same song set in the Psalter, headed as from the day the LORD delivered him from all his enemies and from Saul.
Exodus 15:1-18: The song at the sea after Egypt's army is drowned, the pattern for Israel's victory songs.
Deuteronomy 32:1-43: The song of Moses, which also names God the Rock and describes Him coming in fire.
Habakkuk 3:3-15: God comes in storm, flood, and earthquake to save His people and His anointed.
Romans 15:9: Paul quotes verse 50, I will praise You among the Gentiles and sing to Your name.

translationNotes.note: This chapter and Psalm 18 are the same composition, preserved twice in Scripture with small differences of wording, and the psalm's own heading names the same occasion: the day the LORD delivered David from all his enemies and from Saul. That is worth knowing because it shows how Israel's songs travelled, kept both inside the history that produced them and inside the collection used for worship. Seventy-three psalms carry David's name in their headings.

Verses 8 to 16 do not describe the weather at any battle in the book. Earth shaking, smoke from the nostrils, fire from the mouth, thick darkness under His feet, hailstones and coals, the channels of the sea laid bare: this is the vocabulary of Sinai (Exodus 19:16-18, 20:21), and Deborah's song reaches for it too when the LORD goes out from Seir (Judges 5:4-5). The song is claiming that the God who came down on the mountain is the one who came down for this man.

Verse 35 is about arms, not metallurgy. A war bow of this period was composite, built from wood, horn and sinew glued in layers, and it took real strength to string and hold at full draw; that is the point of a bow described as bronze. The line before it says He trains my hands for battle, so the boast is that the strength is issued, not owned. The Hebrew literally has the arms bending a bow of bronze.

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

The song calls God a rock, a fortress, a shield, a horn, and a stronghold, and every one is a piece of hill country warfare rather than poetry for its own sake. A tsur is a cliff or crag, the kind of ground David actually hid in at En-gedi and Maon, where a small force cannot be surrounded. Moses uses the same title six times in Deuteronomy 32.

stories.keyTakeaway: David recites a song of thanksgiving to the LORD for delivering him from his enemies and from Saul, describing God's power through vivid imagery of divine intervention and declaring his own righteousness and military victories.

stories.title: ⛰️ 2 Samuel 23
summaryBullets: These are the last words of David: “The oracle of David son of Jesse, the oracle of the man raised on high, the one anointed by the God of Jacob, and the sweet psalmist of Israel: (23:1).
The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me; His word was on my tongue. (23:2).
The God of Israel spoke; the Rock of Israel said to me, ‘He who rules the people with justice, who rules in the fear of God, (23:3).
is like the light of the morning at sunrise of a cloudless dawn, the glistening after the rain on the sprouting grass of the earth.’ (23:4).
Is not my house right with God? For He has established with me an everlasting covenant, ordered and secured in every part. Will He not bring about my full salvation and my every desire? (23:5).
But the worthless are all like thorns raked aside, for they can never be gathered by hand. (23:6).
The man who touches them must be armed with iron or with the shaft of a spear. The fire burns them to ashes in the place where they lie.” (23:7).
These are the names of David’s mighty men: Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite was chief of the Three. He wielded his spear against eight hundred men, whom he killed at one time. (23:8).

Next in command was Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite. As one of the three mighty men, he went with David to taunt the Philistines who had gathered for battle at Pas-dammim. The men of Israel retreated, (23:9).

but Eleazar stood his ground and struck the Philistines until his hand grew weary and stuck to his sword. The LORD brought about a great victory that day. Then the troops returned to him, but only to plunder the dead. (23:10).
And after him was Shammah son of Agee the Hararite. When the Philistines had banded together near a field full of lentils, Israel’s troops fled from them. (23:11).
But Shammah took his stand in the middle of the field, defended it, and struck down the Philistines. So the LORD brought about a great victory. (23:12).
At harvest time, three of the thirty chief men went down to David at the cave of Adullam, while a company of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim. (23:13).
At that time David was in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was at Bethlehem. (23:14).
David longed for water and said, “Oh, that someone would get me a drink of water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem!” (23:15).

So the three mighty men broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem, and brought it back to David. But he refused to drink it; instead , he poured it out to the LORD, (23:16).
saying, “Far be it from me, O LORD, to do this! Is this not the blood of the men who risked their lives?” So he refused to drink it. Such were the exploits of the three mighty men. (23:17).
Now Abishai, the brother of Joab and son of Zeruiah, was chief of the Three, and he wielded his spear against three hundred men, killed them, and won a name along with the Three. (23:18).
Was he not more honored than the Three? And he became their commander, even though he was not included among the Three. (23:19).
And Benaiah son of Jehoiada was a man of valor from Kabzeel, a man of many exploits. He struck down two champions of Moab, and on a snowy day he went down into a pit and killed a lion. (23:20).

He also struck down an Egyptian, a huge man. Although the Egyptian had a spear in his hand, Benaiah went against him with a club, snatched the spear from his hand, and killed the Egyptian with his own spear. (23:21).
These were the exploits of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who won a name along with the three mighty men. (23:22).
He was most honored among the Thirty, but he did not become one of the Three. And David appointed him over his guard. (23:23).
Now these were members of the Thirty: Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan son of Dodo of Bethlehem, (23:24).
Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite, (23:25).
Helez the Paltite, Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, (23:26).
Abiezer the Anathothite, Mebunnai the Hushathite, (23:27).
Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite, (23:28).
Heled son of Baanah the Netophathite, Ittai son of Ribai from Gibeah of the Benjamites, (23:29).
Benaiah the Pirathonite, Hiddai from the brooks of Gaash, (23:30).
Abi-albon the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Barhumite, (23:31).
Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan (23:32).
son of Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam son of Sharar the Hararite, (23:33).
Eliphelet son of Ahasbai the Maacathite, Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite, (23:34).
Hezro the Carmelite, Paarai the Arbite, (23:35).
Igal son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite, (23:36).
Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite, the armor-bearer of Joab son of Zeruiah, (23:37).
Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite, (23:38).
and Uriah the Hittite. There were thirty-seven in all. (23:39).
crossRefs: 1 Chronicles 11:10-47: The parallel roll of David's mighty men, with a further list of names at the end.
2 Samuel 7:12-16: The covenant these last words call everlasting, ordered in all things and secure.
Numbers 15:5,10: The drink offering poured out to the LORD alongside the burnt offering.
Micah 5:2: Bethlehem, little among the clans of Judah, from which the ruler of Israel comes.
Psalm 72:1-7: The king who rules in the fear of God is like the light of morning and like rain on the mown grass.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נְאֻם (neum), oracle - נְעִים זְמִרוֹת (neim zemirot), the sweet singer
translationNotes.note: Verse 1 introduces the poem with neum, the formal word for a prophetic utterance, the same one used in the phrase declares the LORD throughout the prophets, and Balaam's oracles at Numbers 24:3. It then gives David four titles in a row: son of Jesse, the man raised on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, and the sweet singer of Israel. Verse 2 states the claim directly, that the Spirit of the LORD spoke by him and His word was on his tongue.

Verses 8 to 39 are a formal roll of honour with two ranks in it, the Three at the top and the Thirty below, each with named captains, and it works the way a decorations list works: a man is admitted for a specific recorded action, so each entry gives the deed. It closes at verse 39 with the total, thirty-seven in all, and with one last name, Uriah the Hittite. The writer sets it there and says nothing about it.

translationNotes.term: Benaiah and the lion in the pit
translationNotes.note: Verse 20 credits Benaiah with three things, and the middle one needs unpacking. The Hebrew says he struck down two ariels of Moab, a word built from lion and God; English versions render it champions, and what the title actually designated is not known. Then he went down into a pit on a snowy day and killed a lion, which tells you both that cisterns were deep rock-cut shafts a man had to climb into, and that snow falls in the Judean hills in winter. Verse 23 makes him commander of David's bodyguard, and 1 Kings 2:35 makes him commander of the whole army under Solomon.

translationNotes.term: Poured it out to the LORD
translationNotes.note: Three men break through a Philistine garrison to fetch water from the well at Bethlehem, and David will not drink it (verses 15 to 17). Pouring a liquid out on the ground before God was the drink offering that went with the daily sacrifices (Numbers 15:5-10). He treats water bought at that risk as something only God has a right to.

stories.keyTakeaway: David delivers his final words affirming God's covenant with him and promising judgment for evil men. He then catalogs his mighty warriors, listing their individual exploits and naming all thirty-seven of his chief fighters.

stories.title: ⛰️ 2 Samuel 24
summaryBullets: Again the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He stirred up David against them, saying, “Go and take a census of Israel and Judah.” (24:1).
So the king said to Joab the commander of his army, who was with him, “Go now throughout the tribes of Israel from Dan to Beersheba and register the troops, so that I may know their number.” (24:2).

But Joab replied to the king, “May the LORD your God multiply the troops a hundred times over, and may the eyes of my lord the king see it. But why does my lord the king want to do such a thing?” (24:3).

Nevertheless , the king’s word prevailed against Joab and against the commanders of the army. So Joab and the commanders of the army departed from the presence of the king to register the troops of Israel. (24:4).
They crossed the Jordan and camped near Aroer, south of the town in the middle of the valley, and proceeded toward Gad and Jazer. (24:5).
Then they went to Gilead and the land of Tahtim-hodshi, and on to Dan-jaan and around to Sidon. (24:6).
They went toward the fortress of Tyre and all the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites. Finally, they went on to the Negev of Judah, to Beersheba. (24:7).
At the end of nine months and twenty days, having gone through the whole land, they returned to Jerusalem. (24:8).
And Joab reported to the king the total number of the troops. In Israel there were 800,000 men of valor who drew the sword, and in Judah there were 500,000. (24:9).

After David had numbered the troops, his conscience was stricken and he said to the LORD, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done. Now, O LORD, I beg You to take away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.” (24:10).
When David got up in the morning, the word of the LORD had come to Gad the prophet, David’s seer: (24:11).
“Go and tell David that this is what the LORD says: ‘I am offering you three options. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you.’” (24:12).

So Gad went and said to David, “Do you choose to endure three years of famine in your land, three months of fleeing the pursuit of your enemies, or three days of plague upon your land? Now then, think it over and decide how I should reply to Him who sent me.” (24:13).
David answered Gad, “I am deeply distressed. Please, let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men.” (24:14).
So the LORD sent a plague upon Israel from that morning until the appointed time, and seventy thousand of the people from Dan to Beersheba died. (24:15).

But when the angel stretched out his hand to destroy Jerusalem, the LORD relented from the calamity and said to the angel who was destroying the people, “Enough! Withdraw your hand now!” At that time the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. (24:16).

When David saw the angel striking down the people, he said to the LORD, “Surely I, the shepherd, have sinned and acted wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done? Please, let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house.” (24:17).
And that day Gad came to David and said to him, “Go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.” (24:18).
So David went up at the word of Gad, just as the LORD had commanded. (24:19).
When Araunah looked out and saw the king and his servants coming toward him, he went out and bowed facedown before the king. (24:20).

“Why has my lord the king come to his servant?” Araunah said. “To buy your threshing floor,” David replied, “that I may build an altar to the LORD, so that the plague upon the people may be halted.” (24:21).
Araunah said to David, “May my lord the king take whatever seems good to him and offer it up. Here are the oxen for a burnt offering and the threshing sledges and ox yokes for the wood. (24:22).
O king, Araunah gives all these to the king.” He also said to the king, “May the LORD your God accept you.” (24:23).

“No,” replied the king, “I insist on paying a price, for I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. (24:24).
And there he built an altar to the LORD and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then the LORD answered the prayers on behalf of the land, and the plague upon Israel was halted. (24:25).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֹּפֶר נֶפֶשׁ (kopher nephesh), a ransom for a life
translationNotes.note: Nothing in this chapter makes sense without Exodus 30:11-16, and no modern reader has it to hand. That law says when a census of Israel is taken, every man counted must pay half a shekel as a ransom for his life to the LORD, rich and poor alike, so that there be no plague among them when they are numbered. A count of fighting men treats the nation as an asset belonging to the king, and the half-shekel is the standing reminder that it belongs to God. Joab's objection in verse 3 is made without argument, and he is right.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַיַּךְ לֵב־דָּוִד (vayyakh lev David), and David's heart struck him
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew in verse 10 says David's heart struck him, using nakah, the ordinary verb for hitting or striking down. The same expression is used once before in his life, at 1 Samuel 24:5, after he cut the corner off Saul's robe in the cave. Both times it comes after the act and before anyone accuses him, and both times what follows is a confession in plain words: I have sinned greatly in what I have done.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גֹּרֶן אֲרַוְנָה (goren Aravnah), the threshing floor of Araunah
translationNotes.note: A threshing floor is a flat, hard, open circle of levelled rock, sited high and clear so the wind can carry the chaff off, and there was one on the rise just north of the old city, still owned by a Jebusite. Verse 24 has David refuse to take it as a gift, saying he will not offer to the LORD what costs him nothing, and pay for the floor and the oxen. 2 Chronicles 3:1 records what was built on that ground afterwards: Solomon's temple, on Mount Moriah, on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֲמִשִּׁים שְׁקָלִים כֶּסֶף (chamishim sheqalim kesef)
translationNotes.note: Verse 24 records the price as fifty shekels of silver, about a pound and a quarter of it, and says exactly what it bought: the threshing floor and the oxen, that is, the working surface and the animals for the sacrifice. 1 Chronicles 21:25 records a second and much larger payment, six hundred shekels of gold, and says what that bought: the site. One is the price of a floor and a pair of oxen; the other is the price of the ground the temple would stand on.

The census route in verses 2 to 8 runs from Dan at the northern springs under Mount Hermon to Beersheba in the dry south, about 150 miles apart, and it took Joab nine months and twenty days. The phrase is Israel's standard way of saying the whole country, from one end to the other. Counting fighting men over that whole span is what makes this a military census.

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD incites David to take a census; after Joab completes the count of Israel's fighting men, David repents and chooses plague as his punishment, which kills seventy thousand people before stopping at Jerusalem. David buys Araunah's threshing floor, builds an altar, and offers sacrifices, and the plague ceases.

intro:
2 Samuel was written by the prophets Nathan and Gad, who served as court prophets during David's reign, with their records and Samuel's earlier material compiled together as recorded in 1 Chronicles 29:29: "the acts of King David, from first to last, are written in the records of Samuel the seer, the records of Nathan the prophet, and the records of Gad the seer." Since Samuel had died before David became king over all Israel (1 Samuel 25:1), the material covering the full forty-year reign came primarily from Nathan and Gad. The book reached its final form around 970-960 BC, during or shortly after the close of David's reign in Jerusalem. Nathan was the court prophet under David, the one who confronted David over Bathsheba and Uriah, who delivered the Davidic covenant promise, and who later helped install Solomon as king (1 Kings 1). Gad was David's personal seer, who advised him from the early cave-fugitive years through the end of his reign. The events of the book cover 1011 to 971 BC, spanning David's forty-year reign, first over Judah from Hebron (seven and a half years), then over a united Israel from Jerusalem (thirty-three years), after he had conquered the Jebusite stronghold and made it his capital. The historical setting is the beginning of Iron Age IIA in Canaan, with the United Monarchy of Israel emerging as a regional power; David subjugated the Philistines (Gath, Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron) along the coastal plain, the Moabites east of the Dead Sea, the Edomites of Mount Seir, the Ammonites of Rabbah, and the Aramaean kingdoms of Damascus and Zobah, extending Israelite influence from the brook of Egypt to the upper Euphrates. To the south, Egypt's 21st Dynasty (the Tanite kings) ruled a weakened, fractured state, while Assyria in the north was in a period of decline before its later resurgence.

2 Samuel and 1 Samuel were originally a single Hebrew book called Shmuel ("Samuel"), divided by the Greek Septuagint translators (3rd century BC) and grouped with Kings as "1-4 Kingdoms" (or "Reigns"); the Latin Vulgate inherited the division with the names "1-2 Samuel" and "1-2 Kings," and English Bibles followed this arrangement. In the Jewish canon, Samuel is the third book of the Former Prophets (Nevi'im Rishonim). Hebrew manuscript fragments of Samuel were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the 3rd century BC and later.
